title: Install Choro and complete setup
summary: Install Choro on your Mac and use the introductory tour to learn the workspace.
before: Have access to a coding provider and a local project folder. The introductory Playground is separate from your normal workspace.
steps: Visit https://choro.dev and use Download to get the current Mac release. Use the system requirements shown with that release.
Open the downloaded disk image, copy Choro to Applications, and launch Choro from Applications.
In the welcome tour, choose Build something. Select the tools and coding providers you use, then check their connection statuses.
Follow the guided Playground steps through agent work, docs, tasks, and the running project. Review each result before advancing.
Choose Start working when you are ready, then Add project to select your own local folder. You can also exit the tour and begin with an existing project.
outcome: Choro opens your workspace, and your selected project appears in the sidebar.
troubleshooting: If a provider says Not installed or Sign in needed, finish that provider’s setup before sending an agent task. If macOS refuses to launch the app, record the exact message and contact support; do not disable system security as a routine setup step.

title: Connect your coding provider
summary: Use a coding provider you already have access to, then choose it for new work.
before: Choro supports Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode configurations. Provider availability depends on your local installation and sign-in state.
steps: During setup, select the providers you use and read each status: Connected, Sign in needed, Not installed, or Status unavailable.
Complete installation or authentication through that provider’s own supported flow when needed. Return to Choro after signing in.
Open Settings → AI generation. Under New agents, choose the provider, model, and available effort level you want as your default.
Open New Agent in a project and check the composer’s provider and model before sending a small request.
outcome: The agent starts with your selected provider; future new agents use your saved default unless you override it.
troubleshooting: Changing the model does not repair an expired login. Follow the sign-in guidance shown in Choro, then retry the failed request. Settings for Quick Ask and Quick generation are separate from New agents.

title: Add your first project
summary: Add a local folder so its files and agent work have a project home in Choro.
before: Choose the folder containing the project you intend to work on. Git-based actions require a Git repository; browsing a folder does not.
steps: Click Add project in the sidebar, or use its configured shortcut (⌘O by default).
Select the project folder in the macOS folder picker. Grant folder access if macOS requests it.
Select the new project in the sidebar and open Code to confirm that the expected files are present.
Open New Agent only after checking the project name. Start with a small question about the folder to confirm the scope.
outcome: The project remains in the sidebar so you can return to its files, tasks, docs, and conversations.
troubleshooting: If files are missing, check whether you selected a parent folder or a nested subproject. If access is denied, review macOS folder permissions for Choro. Do not move or remove the underlying project just to troubleshoot its sidebar entry.

title: Complete your first agent task
summary: Complete a small agent task, inspect its result, and continue with a focused follow-up.
before: Add a project and use a connected provider. Choose a task whose result you can check, such as explaining a module or changing one label.
steps: Select the project and open New Agent (⌘N by default). Check the provider, model, effort, and access choice.
Describe the desired outcome and any limits. For example: “Explain the main entry point and the command used to run this project. Do not change files.”
Send the request. Read progress and respond to any question or approval that needs your decision.
Read the final response. For an implementation task, open Changed Files and inspect the diff. Complete any relevant What to check items.
Send a specific follow-up if the result misses a requirement. Use Git or Ship only when the changes are ready for delivery.
outcome: You have a saved conversation and a result you have reviewed, with any implementation changes available to inspect.
troubleshooting: An agent finishing a turn is not proof that the task works. If the response reports a test it could not run, perform that check before shipping. Do not send the same task repeatedly while its original run is still active.

title: Find your way around the workspace
summary: Find the project, conversation, files, and supporting tools you need.
before: Open a project. Tool placement can vary with your window layout and the project tools you have enabled.
steps: Use the left sidebar to switch projects and open their agent conversations. Check the project name and branch in the header.
Use the project tool rail to switch among Agents, Code, Tasks, and Docs. Use Manage to choose additional project tools when needed.
In Code, select a file from the file browser. Open a terminal or use Run for a saved script.
Use Preview to inspect a running project beside your work, and Git to inspect repository changes.
Open Settings for preferences that apply across the workspace, including AI generation, Band, shortcuts, and backups.
outcome: You can move between a task, its agent, and the underlying project without changing projects accidentally.
troubleshooting: If a tool is absent from the rail, inspect Manage before assuming its data is missing. When a file or conversation looks unfamiliar, confirm the active project and any Solo scope.

title: Choose between Quick Ask, Project Talk, and an agent
summary: Choose the conversation type that matches the amount of action you want.
before: Quick Ask and Project Talk are useful for understanding and discussion. Use an agent when you want implementation work.
steps: Choose Quick Ask for a focused question. Project scope uses the active project; General scope is for questions that do not need repository context.
Choose Project Talk for a read-only conversation about the project, including spoken discussion after voice setup.
Choose New Agent for implementation, ongoing investigation, or a plan you intend to turn into code.
Use Plan mode when the implementation approach needs agreement first. Use Band when you explicitly want a lead to coordinate delegated assignments.
outcome: The conversation starts with a scope and level of action that match your intent.
troubleshooting: Quick Ask’s Start agent action prepares an unsent draft. Review that draft before sending; asking a question alone does not authorize implementation. Project Talk audio processing and coding-provider text processing have different data-handling scopes.

title: Organize and customize your projects
summary: Make important projects easy to recognize and return to.
before: Project organization changes Choro’s navigation; it does not move your repository folders.
steps: Open the project’s sidebar menu. Use its favorite action to make a frequently used project easier to return to; a current favorite offers Remove from Favorites.
Use Move to Section to place the project in an existing sidebar group. Expand the section before looking for the project again.
Choose Rename when its sidebar label needs to be clearer. Choose Customize icon to give it a recognizable symbol and color.
Check the active project name in the header after switching. Sidebar organization does not change the repository folder or its Git branch.
Use Manage on the tool rail to show the tools you need for that project, such as Assets.
outcome: Projects are easier to scan, while their files remain in their original folders.
troubleshooting: If a project seems absent, expand its section and inspect the sidebar filter. Removing a favorite only changes its navigation placement; it does not delete the project.

title: Find files, tasks, docs, and conversations
summary: Search project files and work records without opening every tool separately.
before: Select the project whose work you want to search. File indexing may take a moment for a newly added folder.
steps: Select the intended project and open Search from the sidebar.
Enter a distinctive word from the work, such as activation in the demo. Start with All to see the available result types.
Use Files, Chats, Tasks, or Docs to narrow the results. Check each result’s type and surrounding text before opening it.
Open a result and confirm that it belongs to the expected project and work item. Return to Search and refine the query if you chose a similarly named item.
Use Find in current view when you need a match inside the document or editor you are already reading.
outcome: The selected result opens in its relevant workspace view.
troubleshooting: If nothing matches, confirm the project and filter, shorten the query, and wait for indexing to finish. Generated folders such as node_modules are excluded from file discovery; project search is not a promise to search every byte on disk.

title: Add project assets and references
summary: Keep reusable images and links with the project as Assets.
before: Use references that are relevant to the project and that your agent is permitted to access.
steps: Open Assets in the project’s tool rail. If it is hidden, open Manage and enable Assets.
Choose Add and select the appropriate source: Image, Paste screenshot, Figma or URL, or File.
For a web reference, choose Figma or URL and fill in a descriptive Title and the Source URL. Use Notes to explain why the reference matters.
Choose a folder if appropriate, then Add. Open the resulting asset and check its title, source, and notes.
Use Open to inspect the source or Edit to correct its details. A site may not allow an embedded preview, so a blank embed does not necessarily mean the saved URL is incorrect.
Choose Use in Agent to bring the asset into an agent draft. Add the specific task and explain which aspects of the reference to follow before sending.
outcome: The reference is available in the project instead of being buried in one conversation.
troubleshooting: A saved link does not grant access to a private website. If the agent cannot read it, provide an accessible reference or the relevant content. Keep source files available when an asset points to a local path.

title: Attach files, images, and links to a request
summary: Give an agent the evidence it needs alongside the request.
before: Select the destination project before attaching an image. Use only the files and references needed for this task.
steps: In the composer, type @ to select files or folders, or @@ to select a project doc. Use the picker rather than relying on an ambiguous filename.
Attach or paste an image and wait for attachment processing to finish.
For a URL, include it in the brief and explain which part is relevant. Mention whether a screenshot is a visual reference or a bug example.
Review the context and message together, then send. For example: “Use this screenshot for spacing and hierarchy; keep our current text and colors.”
outcome: The sent request contains the context and instructions needed to interpret it.
troubleshooting: If sending is blocked while an image attaches, wait for completion or resolve the attachment error. A reference alone does not explain what should change; add an explicit outcome.

title: Create and manage project memories
summary: Save concise project facts that should guide later agent work.
before: Use project memory for information specific to one repository. Select the intended project before saving, and keep temporary task details in the conversation or requirement document.
steps: Open Settings → Brain → Memories. Choose Project and confirm the project in the selector.
Choose New memory and write one short, self-contained fact. Include enough context that a future agent can understand it without rereading the original conversation.
For example, the demo records that its Verify script checks required file presence only, while browser behavior and keyboard access still need manual checks.
Choose Save, then read the saved row to confirm its text and scope. Edit it if the statement is ambiguous or no longer accurate.
Use Pin to prioritize an important fact. Use On/Off when you want to control inclusion while keeping the memory saved.
You can also explicitly ask a project agent to remember a repository fact. Review any suggested memory before accepting it, and check the saved result in Settings.
outcome: The enabled memory becomes project context for later agent work. Global preferences remain a separate scope.
troubleshooting: Memory supplies context; it does not enforce behavior or prove a claim is still true. Prefer a few useful facts over repeated or contradictory instructions. If an agent appears to miss a fact, check the selected project and whether the memory is enabled. Update obsolete facts rather than leaving conflicting versions.

title: Manage memories that apply across projects
summary: Save preferences that should apply across your projects.
before: Choose Global only for information that is useful beyond one repository. Keep architecture, project paths, and local run commands in project memories.
steps: Open Settings → Brain → Memories and choose Global.
Choose New memory. Write one clear preference, such as “Explain the result first, then list any checks that remain.”
Choose Save and check the resulting row. Global scope should be visible so you do not mistake the preference for a fact about the selected repository.
Use Pin for an especially useful preference and On/Off to control whether the saved memory is included.
Use Edit when a preference changes. Revisit the list periodically so outdated instructions do not conflict with your current expectations.
outcome: Enabled global memories provide shared context across projects. A disabled memory remains saved for later use.
troubleshooting: Add global preferences explicitly in Settings. The project memory tool available to agents creates project memories, not global ones. Keep each entry self-contained and avoid including project-specific secrets or paths in a preference intended for every project. A memory is guidance for future work, not an automatic correction to existing conversations.

title: Use Knowledge to find previous decisions
summary: Use Knowledge to revisit summaries of earlier project work.
before: Knowledge contains agent summaries rather than a complete copy of every conversation. Use it to find prior context, then verify important details against the original work and current files.
steps: Open Settings → Brain → Knowledge.
Choose the project whose previous work you want to inspect. Check the project filter before assuming a summary is missing.
Search for a distinctive term from the task, outcome, or decision. Try a broader phrase if the exact wording does not produce a match.
Read a relevant summary and identify the outcome, limitations, and follow-up work it describes.
Compare the recalled decision with the current repository or original conversation before relying on it for a new change. Explain any new constraints when you start the next agent request.
outcome: You can recover useful context from past work without treating an old summary as the current source of truth.
troubleshooting: An empty project view is expected until summaries are available. Choro’s empty state explains that summaries appear after an agent finishes, ships, or rejoins. The screenshot shows that initial state and its search and project controls. Changing the project filter may reveal a different set of summaries; an empty view is not proof that all conversation history is gone.

title: Start and configure an agent
summary: Start an agent in the right project with a clear request and a suitable configuration.
before: Add the project first and make sure your coding provider is available. A new conversation uses the selected project; creating a chat alone does not create an isolated copy of its files.
steps: Select the project and open New Agent. Check the project name under the composer before writing the request.
Open the model control and choose the provider and model. Choose an available reasoning effort for the task; the options depend on the model.
Review the access control separately. Choose how much supervision the agent should need for file changes and other operations.

Write a concrete request: the expected behavior, relevant context, limits, and how the result should be checked. For example, ask for a clearer empty state and specify the action users should take when there are no updates.
Attach relevant files, docs, or images through the composer. Keep the request focused on the material the agent needs, and confirm that linked requirements belong to this project.
If you need an approach before implementation, focus the composer and press Shift+Tab to enable Plan. Check that the Plan chip is visible. Otherwise keep the default working mode.
Read the whole draft, then send it. Follow the resulting conversation, answer questions, and inspect the work before deciding it is complete.
outcome: A new agent conversation starts with the selected project, configuration, and request. Its progress and results remain in that conversation.
troubleshooting: If Choro asks you to choose a project or describe the task, complete that part of the draft before sending. Check provider availability when no model can be selected. For simultaneous implementation that must stay separate, consider Solo; two ordinary conversations can work in the same project folder.

title: Choose a provider, model, and reasoning effort
summary: Choose the provider, model, and effort for a particular agent request.
before: Use a provider you already have installed and signed in to. The model picker reflects what Choro can offer through each provider; picking a model does not sign you in or create provider access.
steps: Open New Agent in the intended project, then click the model name in the composer.
Choose the provider in the picker and inspect its model list. Select the model you intend to use. Provider and model are a combined choice in this control.
Check the model name shown in the composer after selection. This catches a common mistake: selecting a provider while assuming the previous model still applies.
Open the effort control, when available, and choose a supported level. More deliberation can help with work involving several constraints, but can also take more time and provider resources.
Review access and Plan mode separately. A different model does not by itself grant additional permissions or turn an implementation request into a planning request.
Send the task when the configuration matches your intent. For future defaults, open Settings → AI generation → New agents; Quick Ask and Quick generation have separate preferences.
outcome: The composer shows the configuration that will be used for the request. You can use a task-specific choice without assuming every future conversation should use the same one.
troubleshooting: Model lists and effort choices can differ between providers and change as provider support evolves. Follow the labels available in your installation rather than looking for a particular model from this screenshot. If OpenCode has no selectable models, check its local configuration. Resolve authentication errors in the relevant provider instead of repeatedly choosing the same unavailable model.

title: Understand agent access and approvals
summary: Choose how an agent handles permissions and respond to approval requests deliberately.
before: Check the access control in the composer before sending. Access describes permission behavior; Plan describes the kind of work you are asking for. They are separate controls.
steps: Open the access menu in the composer and read the available choices. Labels differ by provider, so confirm the selected provider first.

For Codex, Ask for approval requests supervision for operations; Approve for me allows routine trusted actions while asking about actions detected as potentially unsafe. Full access permits unrestricted file and internet access without those prompts.
For Claude, the corresponding labels are Supervised, Auto-accept edits, and Full access. Auto-accept edits permits file edits automatically while other actions can still need a decision.
Choose the mode that matches the work and the supervision you want. A request to inspect code is still a task instruction; it is not the same as selecting a permission boundary.
When an approval card appears, read the actual operation and target. Approve only the requested action you intend to allow, or decline it and explain a suitable alternative.
If work cannot continue, inspect the reported error. Distinguish a denied permission from missing credentials, an unavailable tool, or an incorrect project before choosing the next step.
outcome: The agent operates under the selected provider’s access behavior and your individual decisions. You remain responsible for reviewing the resulting changes.
troubleshooting: Approving a plan permits implementation of an approach; approving an operation permits a specific action. Neither proves the result is correct. Full access does not supply missing credentials or guarantee every integration will run. Provider policies can still affect particular tools, so use the actual error as the starting point for recovery.

title: Plan a task before implementation
summary: Agree on the approach before an agent starts implementation.
before: Use Plan when the requirements, architecture, or scope need discussion. Open the intended project and confirm the provider and model before sending the planning request.
steps: Focus the new-agent composer and press Shift+Tab to turn on Plan. The Plan chip appears beside the other controls. If you customized shortcuts, check the binding in Settings → Keyboard shortcuts.

Describe the outcome and constraints, then ask the agent to inspect the relevant code before proposing changes. For example: “Plan keyboard navigation improvements for the client portal. Identify affected files and checks. Do not implement changes yet.”
Send the request and follow the investigation. Read any clarifying question and answer it specifically; a useful plan depends on the right requirements.
When the plan card appears, choose Expand plan to read more than its opening section. Check the affected files, proposed steps, assumptions, and verification approach.
Ask for a revision if the scope is wrong or an important requirement is missing. Explain the correction and what the revised plan should preserve.
When the approach is ready, use the plan’s implementation decision. Treat that choice as permission to begin the described work, then review the actual implementation against the plan.
outcome: The conversation retains the proposed approach and your decision. A completed planning response is a preparation step; it is not evidence that the feature has been implemented.
troubleshooting: The Plan chip is shown after Plan mode is enabled, so its absence in a fresh composer is expected. Clicking an active Plan chip returns to the default working mode. For Band delegation, planning belongs to the lead; specialists can provide focused analysis. Plan approval is separate from individual tool permissions and from checking the final result.

title: Understand agent statuses and activity cards
summary: Read the conversation’s status and cards to decide what needs your attention.
before: Choro shows both a workflow status and live execution activity. Read them together: an In progress workflow can remain after the provider finishes a turn.
steps: Open the conversation and read the latest activity. Working or Reviewing with an elapsed time describes an active provider pass; a spinner or stop control also signals activity.
Use Needs attention in the sidebar to find conversations waiting for a decision or a result you should review. Open the specific question, plan, approval, or error before responding.
Read the final response and supporting cards. Files changed, What to check, verification, and Code review each answer different questions about the result.
Open the workflow status menu when you need to organize the work. Its choices include Backlog, To do, In progress, Done, and Rejected.
Choose a workflow status deliberately after reviewing the outcome. Marking work Done is not a substitute for running checks, committing, or shipping.
For Band, inspect assignment states as well as the lead conversation. One Bandmate finishing does not mean the combined task is integrated or verified.
outcome: You can distinguish active execution, a decision needing attention, and your own workflow classification.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows an In progress workflow after a code-review result. That combination is possible and does not by itself mean the provider is still running. Inspect the latest activity and decision cards before repeatedly sending Continue. A clean review can coexist with an unchecked manual checklist.

title: Answer questions and approve a plan
summary: Unblock an agent by answering the decision it is actually waiting for.
before: Open the conversation that needs attention and read the preceding messages. A question, a plan decision, and an operation approval ask for different kinds of input.
steps: Read the question or decision card in full. For a question, choose the answer that matches your requirement, or write a specific answer when the offered choices do not cover it.
For a plan, open Expand plan and inspect the proposed scope, affected files, implementation steps, and checks. Do not judge a long plan only by its opening paragraph.
If the plan needs changes, choose “No, tell the agent what to do differently” and describe the correction. Name the missing requirement or unwanted change so the agent can revise its approach.
If the plan is ready, choose “Yes, implement this plan” and the Implement action. This starts implementation of the proposed approach; it does not mark the work as verified or shipped.
If the card instead asks for an operation permission, read the command or action and its target. Approve or decline that specific operation according to what you intend to allow.
After submitting a decision, look for the next activity in the same conversation. Review subsequent questions separately: an answer to one decision may not resolve another.
outcome: The agent receives an actionable answer and can continue the intended work. The plan and surrounding conversation remain available for checking the result later.
troubleshooting: A generic “continue” message may not answer a structured decision card. If work still needs attention, read the current card and any provider error before repeating your answer. Dismiss is not the same as approving implementation. Approving a plan does not waive later permission requests, prove tests passed, or authorize shipping.

title: Stop, resume, or continue a conversation
summary: Pause active work or continue a saved conversation with its existing context.
before: Stopping work does not undo changes already made. Review the current files before assuming the project is unchanged.
steps: Open the conversation that is currently working and choose Stop when you intend to interrupt it. Allow its activity state to settle before sending another request.
Read the last response and inspect any partial files. Stopping does not revert edits, stop every project service, or undo a completed external action.
When a saved conversation displays Resume this conversation, choose Resume to load its history and reconnect the agent.
Read the restored history and any recovery error. Send a precise follow-up describing what should continue and what requirements have changed.
For delegated work, inspect the lead and its assignments. Use Resume bandmates when the specialist assignments should resume; reopening the lead alone is not the same operation.
Review the next result against the original request and the follow-up. Complete outstanding checks before marking the work done.
outcome: The work continues with its saved conversation context and your updated instructions.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows a saved conversation waiting for Resume, not an active provider run. If reconnecting fails, preserve the error and partial files, check the provider, and retry after addressing the cause. Avoid starting duplicate implementation tasks on the same files while recovery is unresolved.

title: Manage several active agents
summary: Supervise several conversations without losing track of their project or scope.
before: Parallel work is easiest to review when tasks have separate outcomes. Use Solo for implementation that needs its own Git working copy.
steps: Give each agent a task with a clear boundary and recognizable title.
Use project and agent lists to identify active work and conversations needing attention.
Handle questions and approvals in the relevant conversation, then return to the other work.
Review each result independently before combining or shipping changes. Use a lead with Band when assignments need explicit coordination.
outcome: Each conversation remains understandable and its result can be reviewed separately.
troubleshooting: Two ordinary agents in the same project may change the same files. A new conversation is not automatically an isolated workspace. If changes overlap, pause and reconcile them before continuing.

title: Set default models and generation preferences
summary: Choose separate defaults for new agents, Quick Ask, and quick generation.
before: Open Settings → AI generation. The provider must already be installed and signed in; selecting a default does not authenticate it.
steps: Under New agents, select the provider and model you want new conversations to start with. Select an available reasoning effort that suits your usual work. More reasoning can take longer and consume additional provider resources.
Configure Quick Ask separately for lightweight questions. Its model does not have to match the one used for implementation work.
Review Quick generation for the smaller generation tasks that use this preference. Treat each group as a separate default instead of assuming a change applies everywhere.

Review the preferences for manual review checklists and work verification. Choose whether you want verification to be requested each time, started automatically, or left off, according to the options shown.
Open a fresh New Agent composer and check its displayed model and effort before sending. Override the configuration there when one task needs a different setup.
outcome: Future work starts with the relevant saved default. The composer remains the place to confirm the configuration for the particular task you are about to send.
troubleshooting: If a model is unavailable, check its provider configuration and sign-in state. An existing conversation can retain its own configuration. Automatic verification can require additional time and provider usage; completion still deserves a review of the result.

title: Customize keyboard shortcuts
summary: Make frequently used actions easier to reach with your own keyboard shortcuts.
before: Open Settings → Keyboard shortcuts. Record an existing custom binding before replacing it if you may want to restore it later.
steps: Search for the action by name, such as New Agent or Quick Ask. Use All to browse every action and Modified to inspect only your changes.
Click the shortcut keycap for the action you want to change. Press the new key combination when the control is listening.
If Choro reports a duplicate or reserved combination, choose another binding. A shortcut needs to identify one intended action without colliding with another.
Press Escape to cancel a pending capture. Use Delete to unassign a binding when that is what you intend.
Try the action from the normal workspace. If you want the original binding back, use its restore-default control; use Reset all only when you intend to reset every custom shortcut.
outcome: The action shows its new key combination and can be invoked from the workspace. Guides that quote a default shortcut may differ from your customized setting.
troubleshooting: If the shortcut does not trigger, check whether you are still editing the binding or focused in a text field that consumes it. Search for the action again to verify the saved combination. Do not reset all bindings just to fix one action.

title: Configure notifications
summary: Choose when Choro should notify you about agent decisions and completion.
before: Open Settings → Notifications. App preferences and macOS notification permission are separate: both affect what you receive.
steps: Configure notifications for questions and approvals so you know when an agent needs a decision. These notifications are suppressed while you are already viewing the relevant conversation.
Choose the completion behavior shown in Settings: Never, Background, or Always. Background is useful when you want completion alerts while working elsewhere.
Choose the sound behavior separately. Completion notifications are silent; do not assume every visual notification will produce a sound.
Check Choro’s notification permission in macOS if app settings are enabled but alerts never appear.
Use a real small task to observe the chosen behavior. Return to the conversation to read the result or respond to the decision rather than treating a notification as the full context.
outcome: Choro’s notifications match the type of attention you want. The conversation remains the source of the actual question, plan, and outcome.
troubleshooting: If an alert appears missing, first check whether that conversation was already open, whether completion is set to Background or Never, and whether macOS permits notifications. Repeatedly restarting the same agent task will not repair notification permission.

title: Enable or disable beta features
summary: Choose whether to use optional features that are still in development.
before: Open Settings → Beta features. Read the description of a feature before enabling it; beta behavior can change as the app evolves.
steps: Locate the feature you want to use. For managed Band delegation, turn Delegation on.
When delegation is enabled, review the controls for concurrent Bandmates per lead, concurrent Bandmates across Choro, and work revisions. Start with limits that keep the work easy to follow.
Return to your project and explicitly request the feature. For example, use /delegate and select the Bandmates you want; enabling the toggle does not automatically create a team.
To stop allowing new delegation runs later, turn the toggle off. Existing teams can finish, and their historical chats and results remain available.
If your intention is to pause an already-running team, use that team’s Stop control. The global toggle and an active run’s controls serve different purposes.
outcome: The local preference takes effect without a restart. Saved Bandmate profiles and standalone Bandmate chats remain distinct from managed delegation.
troubleshooting: If delegation is unavailable, check this toggle before changing providers or creating duplicate profiles. Importing a workspace archive does not automatically enable delegation. Existing Stop and Resume controls can remain available when the toggle is off.

title: Export a backup
summary: Export a workspace archive you can retain for backup or transfer.
before: Open Settings → Data backups. A Choro workspace archive should be kept alongside your normal repository and file backups; do not assume it replaces them.
steps: Finish or pause work that you want represented consistently in the backup, then open the export controls in Data backups.
Choose Export and wait for the operation to finish. Keep Choro open until it reports the result.
Find the timestamped choro-workspace-export ZIP file in Downloads. If Downloads cannot be used, check the Desktop fallback and the location reported by the app.
Check the filename, timestamp, and that the file is present before relying on the export. Store a copy in a location appropriate for the workspace information it contains.
Keep older known-good archives until you have established that your new backup is usable. Back up the underlying project folders and Git repositories through your normal process too.
outcome: You have a dated export file that can be selected in Choro’s import workflow. Exporting is separate from uploading or sharing that archive.
troubleshooting: If no file appears, read the export result and check the destination’s available space and write access. Avoid repeatedly clicking Export while one operation is in progress. An archive can contain private workspace content, so review the destination before sharing it.

title: Import a backup
summary: Restore workspace data from a Choro export archive.
before: Import replaces the current Choro workspace data. Export a backup of the current workspace first, and confirm that you have selected the intended archive. Do not use import as a harmless way to preview an unknown backup.
steps: Open Settings → Data backups and review the import description. Make sure your current workspace has a recent export you can locate.
Choose Import and select the Choro workspace export ZIP you intend to restore. Selecting the file starts the import, so check its name and date before confirming the picker.
Allow the operation to finish without closing Choro. The import workflow creates a backup of the current workspace as part of replacement.
Follow the app’s restart or reload guidance so open views reflect the restored data.
After reopening, check several familiar projects, conversations, and documents. Confirm that the underlying local project folders are available at the paths the restored workspace expects.
outcome: The selected archive becomes the restored workspace state. The import is a replacement operation, not a merge of two independent workspaces.
troubleshooting: If the archive is rejected, retain both the original archive and your current backup, and record the error. Do not edit the archive contents or repeatedly import different files into important data to investigate. A restored project entry cannot make a missing repository folder reappear.

title: Set up voice input
summary: Prepare local voice input and choose how spoken conversations behave.
before: Open Settings → Voice. You need a working microphone and permission for Choro to use it. Voice models are downloaded on first use or when you install them from this page.
steps: Read the local-model information and start installation if the required model is not present. Allow the download to finish before testing dictation.
Check the microphone permission when macOS prompts for it. If permission was previously denied, review Choro’s microphone access in macOS settings.
Choose the spoken-feedback behavior offered by Choro: Minimal, Balanced, All, or Off. Pick the level that suits whether you want a spoken discussion or primarily typed results.
Review turn-taking preferences before a longer Project Talk session. More patient turn-taking can help if you pause while thinking.
Try one short, non-sensitive sentence in a message draft and inspect the transcript before sending it. Correct names, file paths, and technical terms that were misheard.
outcome: Voice input produces editable text in the relevant workflow. Local audio processing does not remove the need to review the text before it becomes an agent request.
troubleshooting: If nothing is transcribed, check model installation and microphone permission first. Audio is processed on the Mac and not retained; the Voice page describes transcript retention separately. Once text is sent to a coding provider, that provider handles the request according to its own setup.

title: Manage provider skills
summary: Inspect the reusable skills Choro discovers from your coding providers.
before: Open Settings → Skills. Provider skills and Choro Riffs are different sources of reusable instructions; choose the tab for the source you want to inspect.
steps: Select Codex or Claude to see the skills discovered from that provider. Use search to find a skill by its purpose.
Read the available skill information before using it. A skill can contain workflow instructions and supporting resources, so its name alone is not a complete explanation of what it will do.
If a skill needs installation or editing, use the provider’s supported skill workflow. The list in Choro reflects the provider setup rather than creating a separate provider account.
Return to your agent composer and choose the relevant skill through the available picker or slash workflow. Add a concrete task so the agent knows what the guidance should be applied to.
For guidance you maintain within Choro across projects, consider a Riff in the Choro Riffs tab. For a saved specialist, attach a compatible skill in its Bandmate editor.
outcome: The agent receives reusable guidance alongside the specific task. You still control the project, requested outcome, and any permissions that the work requires.
troubleshooting: If a skill is missing, confirm the provider and its installed skill location before assuming the skill was deleted. If a linked skill becomes unavailable or incompatible, inspect the repair guidance instead of silently replacing it with an unrelated skill.

title: Understand leads, Bandmates, and delegation
summary: Understand how a lead coordinates saved specialists and their assignments.
before: A Bandmate is a saved specialist configuration. A lead is the originating conversation that coordinates delegated work. Managed delegation must be enabled separately from using saved Bandmate profiles.
steps: Open Settings → Band and inspect a profile’s description, provider, model, effort, and enabled state. Choose specialists because their instructions match your task, not just because several profiles are available.
For a single specialist conversation, choose a Bandmate when starting a new chat. That is a standalone chat and does not create a managed team.
For coordinated work, enable Delegation in Beta features and explicitly name or select the Bandmates you want the lead to use.
Give the lead a shared outcome and meaningful boundaries between assignments. The lead determines the work order and verifies the integrated result.
Follow the assignment cards and Band panel. Read each result and the lead’s final review; a Bandmate finishing its own assignment is different from the overall task being complete.
outcome: You can distinguish a saved profile, its standalone conversation, and an assignment coordinated by a lead. Delegated assignments have their own chats and private Git working copies.
troubleshooting: An ordinary request does not automatically authorize a team. Merely mentioning a field such as frontend work is not the same as selecting a specific Bandmate. Explicitly choose the team and keep responsibilities clear. Existing Codex or Claude authentication is used.

title: Create or customize a Bandmate
summary: Save a specialist with a clear role, instructions, and expected result.
before: Open Settings → Band. Built-in Choro profiles are editable, so you can start from an existing specialist or use the available creation action.
steps: Use search to find a nearby role and open Edit, or create a Bandmate for a role you cannot find. Give it a name that is easy to select unambiguously.
In Overview, describe when to use the Bandmate. This description should distinguish its job from other specialists in your Band.
Choose its provider, model, and effort. Make sure that provider is usable in your local setup.
Write job instructions and an expected result. For example, a reviewer should explain findings with file references and distinguish required fixes from suggestions.
Open Skills to attach reusable guidance when needed, then Save the Bandmate. Review the saved list entry before starting a chat with it.
outcome: The saved profile is reusable for future specialist work. A new chat can override its model configuration without requiring you to rewrite the saved role.
troubleshooting: If edits are missing, check whether you saved the Bandmate rather than only applying a skill inside its draft. Cancel discards staged profile edits. Avoid giving multiple profiles nearly identical names when you intend to select them through natural-language delegation.

title: Add skills and Riffs to a Bandmate
summary: Attach reusable guidance to a saved specialist without duplicating all of its instructions.
before: Open Settings → Band, edit the intended Bandmate, and switch to Skills. A skill should support the specialist’s role and fit its provider.
steps: Choose Add skill to open the picker. Browse bundled Choro skills, installed provider skills, or Riffs according to the source you need.
Read a skill before attaching it. Bundled skills can be opened with View to inspect their instructions and source information.
For custom guidance, use the custom-skill form and write a specific, reusable workflow. Choose Apply skill to stage it in the Bandmate draft.
Review the attached list for overlapping or conflicting instructions. A long list of skills is not automatically a better specialist.
Choose Save bandmate to persist the complete configuration. Start a suitable task and inspect whether its result follows the intended guidance.
outcome: The saved Bandmate includes the attached guidance when used. Applying a custom skill inside the editor is an intermediate step; saving the Bandmate completes the change.
troubleshooting: Bundled skills are read-only, while custom guidance can be edited. If a linked skill is missing or incompatible, use the repair guidance. Detaching a skill changes the profile without removing its files. Cancelling the Bandmate editor discards staged changes.

title: Start a standalone chat with a Bandmate
summary: Use a saved specialist directly for a focused conversation.
before: Choose a project and make sure the saved Bandmate is enabled and its provider is connected. Managed delegation is not required for a standalone Bandmate chat.
steps: Open New Agent in the intended project and use the Bandmates picker to select the specialist.
Review the resulting model and effort. Override them for this conversation if the task needs a different compatible configuration.
Write a concrete request. A saved reviewer still needs to know what to review, which files matter, and what kind of result you want.
Choose Plan when you want an approach before implementation, or the appropriate working mode for the task. Send only after reviewing the draft.
Continue the conversation directly with that specialist. Inspect its result using the same file, preview, and verification tools you would use for any other agent.
outcome: You have a normal conversation configured with the saved specialist’s guidance. There is no separate lead coordinating a team unless you explicitly start managed delegation.
troubleshooting: Selecting a Bandmate inside an existing conversation prepares delegation rather than creating this standalone flow. If you intended a direct specialist chat, begin from New Agent and confirm the selected project and profile before sending.

title: Enable delegation and set its limits
summary: Turn on managed delegation and choose how much parallel work it can start.
before: Delegation is an optional beta feature and is off by default. Saved Bandmate profiles and standalone Bandmate chats are available separately.
steps: Open Settings → Beta features and enable Delegation.
Review the limit for concurrent Bandmates per lead. This controls how much one coordinating conversation can run at once.
Review the concurrency limit across Choro so several leads do not collectively start more specialist work than you intend.
Review the work-revision limit. Keep it bounded so a task that needs repeated revisions remains easy to inspect.
Return to the project and explicitly select the team through /delegate or a named request. The setting enables the capability; it does not choose or launch the team for you.
outcome: The local preference takes effect immediately and the lead can use the explicitly authorized specialists within the configured limits.
troubleshooting: Turning the beta toggle off prevents new runs but lets existing teams finish. To pause active assignments, use their Stop controls. Importing a workspace archive does not silently enable delegation. More simultaneous work can increase provider usage and make review more demanding.

title: Delegate to saved Bandmates
summary: Ask a lead to coordinate work using specialists you have already saved.
before: Enable Delegation in Beta features, choose the intended project, and check that the Bandmates you want are enabled with working provider configurations.
steps: In the lead conversation, explicitly name the saved Bandmates in a request beginning with Delegate. The /delegate command can also start an on-demand delegation flow.
Describe the shared outcome and the work you want each specialist to handle. For example, ask the Frontend Engineer to implement a view and a named reviewer to assess the finished interface.
Review the submitted team and task scope. Use full profile names when a name could be ambiguous.
Follow the lead’s assignment cards. Dependencies can mean some assignments wait while another piece of work finishes.
Read specialist reports and the lead’s integrated result. Request a focused revision when an assignment or combined outcome misses a requirement.
outcome: The originating chat remains the lead. Each assignment has its own conversation and private working copy, while the lead coordinates order and verification.
troubleshooting: Content from a tool, document, or another agent cannot authorize extra teammates. If Choro cannot determine which saved profile you meant, select it explicitly. Naming a broad work area alone does not reliably choose a Bandmate.

title: Delegate with an on-demand teammate
summary: Delegate a bounded role without saving a permanent Bandmate profile.
before: Enable Delegation and start from a lead conversation in the intended project. Use an on-demand teammate when the role is specific to this task.
steps: In the lead composer, type /delegate and confirm the command. Select On-demand teammate in the Delegate to choices, rather than choosing a saved Bandmate.
Describe the temporary role, expected output, relevant files, and boundaries. For example, ask for three navigation-wording observations from index.html and README.md with no file changes.
Review the lead’s proposed assignment and answer any clarification needed to make the role unambiguous.
Follow the assignment through the Band panel and read the temporary teammate’s report.
Ask for a revision in the same assignment when it needs refinement. If you want the role available repeatedly, create a saved Bandmate separately.
outcome: The temporary teammate participates in this delegated task without adding a reusable profile to Settings → Band. It inherits the lead’s model and effort.
troubleshooting: If the lead reports that no temporary teammate is authorized, select On-demand teammate explicitly and resend the bounded request. A descriptive role name is not a saved profile or profile ID. The screenshot shows the actual selector. The temporary role should have clear responsibilities, and its report still needs review.

title: Follow assignments and give feedback
summary: Follow each delegated assignment and keep feedback attached to the right work.
before: Open the lead conversation that owns the delegated work. The Band panel is scoped to that lead, so another lead’s assignments appear in its own conversation.
steps: Open the Band composer chip or an assignment card. Use Active and Finished to distinguish current work from completed assignment history.
Select an assignment to open its chat in the side panel. Read the compact brief and use Show full brief when you need the complete instructions and original request.
Check the status and latest activity before deciding whether an assignment needs input. A waiting dependency is different from a failed provider request.
Use the assignment’s conversation for relevant feedback and the lead for changes to the shared outcome or coordination.
Choose All bandmates to return to the assignment list. At narrow widths, Close returns from the main-area panel to the lead.
outcome: You can inspect one specialist’s context without losing the lead’s overview. Multiple assignments to the same Bandmate remain separate records.
troubleshooting: Opening a panel or reading a result does not resume stopped work. Use explicit Resume when you intend to restart it. Check the task title as well as the Bandmate name so feedback goes to the correct assignment.

title: Review Bandmate results
summary: Read specialist reports and check the combined result before accepting a delegated task.
before: Open the relevant lead and choose the completed assignment you want to inspect. A specialist finishing its turn is not the same as successful integration.
steps: Choose View summary for the assignment. Read its outcome, addressed requirements, unfinished work, and checks.
Choose Open conversation to inspect the specialist’s full exchange when the summary leaves out context you need. Look for limitations and checks that could not be performed.
Compare the report with the original brief and the actual files or preview. Ask for a revision when the result misses a requirement.
Follow the integration state separately. Bandmate finished, Integrating, Integrated, and Task complete describe different points in the workflow.
Read the lead’s final verification of the combined work. Perform any remaining manual checks before shipping the overall change.
outcome: You have assessed both the individual assignment and its contribution to the shared result. Corrected reports can retain earlier revisions for context.
troubleshooting: A confident summary does not replace checking the actual behavior. If a report says unfinished work remains, resolve it or explicitly reduce the scope before considering the task complete. Do not merge or ship merely because the active Bandmate count has reached zero.

title: Pause, resume, or end delegation
summary: Pause a delegated team, resume intentionally, or end coordination while keeping its files.
before: Open the lead conversation and inspect which assignments are active. Stopping work and deleting its output are different operations.
steps: Use Stop on the relevant assignment or team control when you want work to pause. Wait for the status to reflect that the provider has stopped.
Read the current brief, activity, and any partial result before deciding what to do next. The lead conversation remains usable while Bandmates are stopped.
Choose Resume on an assignment or Resume bandmates when you intend the stopped work to continue.
If you want to finish coordinating this team without discarding its files, use End delegation · Keep files.
Inspect the retained work and the lead’s current state before starting a new implementation that might overlap it.
outcome: Work resumes only after an explicit action. Ending delegation keeps the files available for review rather than treating an incomplete assignment as if it never happened.
troubleshooting: Opening the Band panel does not resume work. Turning off Delegation in Beta features prevents new runs and is not a substitute for stopping an active team. If a provider cannot resume, address its authentication or configuration error before creating duplicate assignments.

title: Browse and edit project files
summary: Read project files and make focused edits in the Code workspace.
before: Select the intended project before opening Code. If you are working in Solo, confirm the active working copy so you inspect the correct files.
steps: Open Code from the project toolbar and choose a file in Files. Start with a familiar README or source file to confirm the folder is correct.
Read the surrounding code before editing. Use Find in current view for text inside the open file, and project Search when you need to locate another file or work record.
Make a small, coherent edit and check the editor’s save state before switching to a run or review step.
Use Git or Changed Files to inspect the diff rather than relying only on how the final file looks. Confirm that no unrelated text changed.
Run the relevant check or preview for the behavior you changed. Return to the file or ask an agent for a focused follow-up if the result is wrong.
outcome: You can trace a request to its source files and inspect the actual change. The file tree and editor remain scoped to the selected project or working copy.
troubleshooting: If files look unfamiliar, check project selection and Solo scope first. If a file is missing, verify that it is within the opened folder. Avoid editing generated output when the project expects changes in source files.

title: Use the integrated terminal
summary: Run project commands and read their output without leaving Choro.
before: Open the project’s Code workspace. Know what command you intend to run and whether it changes files, starts a service, or only inspects the project.
steps: Open Terminal from Code. Check the working directory in the shell before running a command, especially if you have switched projects or isolated workspaces.
Enter the project’s documented command and inspect its output. For a first orientation, read the README rather than guessing a package manager or run script.
Keep a long-running development server in its own terminal session so its output remains easy to follow.
When output contains a local HTTP or HTTPS address, open the matching service in Preview. Confirm that the page belongs to this project.
Stop a command deliberately when it is no longer needed. Use the relevant session or service control and check that the process has actually ended.
outcome: The terminal provides the command output you need to diagnose runs, tests, and local services alongside the project files.
troubleshooting: An open terminal is not evidence that a command succeeded. Read its exit result and errors. If a command cannot be found, check the project’s environment and installation instructions. Do not paste unknown commands just to clear an error.

title: Create and run saved scripts
summary: Save a repeatable project command and launch it from Run.
before: Choose a command that already works for this project and understand its working directory. Saved scripts are useful for recurring development tasks such as starting a preview.
steps: Select the project and open its Run scripts controls. Inspect existing scripts before adding a duplicate.
Choose Edit scripts… from the Run menu, then Add script. Enter a clear Name and the Command to run. The demo uses Preview and Verify to distinguish its server from its check.

Set the command to match the project’s documented run instructions. The editor has Name and Command fields, not a separate working-directory field. If the command needs a subdirectory, make that explicit in the command.
Save the script and launch it from Run. Read the terminal output and wait for any readiness message before opening the page.
If the command prints a service URL, select it in Preview and verify the expected app appears. Keep the script updated when the project’s run command changes.
outcome: The project has a repeatable run action with its output available in Choro. Saving a script does not install the command’s dependencies.
troubleshooting: If the script exits immediately, read the first error and test its prerequisites. If it starts in the wrong directory, fix the saved configuration rather than repeatedly changing directories by hand. A successful process start does not necessarily mean the service is ready.

title: Stop and restart a project service
summary: Restart a local project service when its configuration or environment changes.
before: Identify the terminal or saved script that owns the service. A browser refresh and a server restart solve different problems.
steps: Read the service’s latest terminal output and note its address. Confirm it belongs to the project and working copy you intend to restart.
Select the terminal that runs the service, focus its output area, and press Control+C when the command supports interruption. Wait for the tab to show that the process has exited.
Use Restart for the exited terminal, or run the saved script or documented start command again. Watch for startup errors, dependency failures, or a changed port.
Select the current address in Preview. Reload the page once the service reports that it is ready.
Check the specific behavior that prompted the restart, rather than treating a successful startup line as proof that the issue is fixed.
outcome: One intended service instance is running and Preview points to its current address.
troubleshooting: A Python development server may print KeyboardInterrupt after Control+C; in that case it reflects the requested interruption. If a port remains occupied, identify the owning process before terminating anything. Do not stop unrelated system processes. If the service starts on another port, update the selected preview instead of repeatedly refreshing the old address.

title: Open a running app in Preview
summary: Inspect your running application beside its code or agent conversation.
before: Start the project using its documented run command or a saved script. Wait until the service is ready and note the local address it reports.
steps: Open Preview beside the project’s Run control. Choro detects HTTP and HTTPS addresses printed by live project terminals and makes them available in the service picker.
Choose the address for the app you want to inspect. If several services are present, use the one that serves the relevant page.
Navigate to the behavior you are checking and compare it with the task’s expected result.
Switch between the relevant agent conversation and Code as needed. The project preview is shared across its chats, so changing conversations does not create a new page instance.
Use Review when you want to attach visual feedback to a specific part of the page. Check the selected destination agent before sending.
outcome: The running app is visible inside the Choro workspace. Its selected URL is stored for the project so you can return to the preview.
troubleshooting: If the page will not load, inspect the terminal and verify that the service is still running. A remembered preview address does not automatically restart a stopped server. Settings and other project tools can hide the preview surface while you use them.

title: Preview a local HTML file
summary: Open a static HTML page from your project without starting a development server.
before: The file must be suitable for direct local viewing. An application that requires a build step or backend still needs its normal run workflow.
steps: Select the project containing the HTML file and confirm its location in Code.
Ask the project agent to open the specific file in Preview, for example: “Open docs/demo.html in Preview so I can review it.”
Inspect the rendered page and check that local styles, images, and scripts behave as expected.
Return to the same preview from another conversation in the project when needed. Choro keeps file and URL preview records at project scope.
If the file depends on server behavior, use the project’s documented local server instead and open its running URL.
outcome: A supported local HTML file appears in the same Preview panel used for running pages. The request identifies an existing file rather than asking the agent to invent a new one.
troubleshooting: If a page is blank or missing resources, confirm the file path and its relative asset paths. Some browser behavior differs for local files; using the appropriate development server can be necessary. The screenshot shows the actual demo index.html loaded from a file URL, with its local path confirmed in the conversation.

title: Send visual feedback to an agent
summary: Attach a precise visual comment to the agent that should act on it.
before: Open the relevant page in Preview and select the project agent that should receive the feedback. The destination is the selected agent when you press Send.
steps: Use Review in Preview. Click one exact page element when the issue concerns that element, or drag a region when the issue spans an area.
Read the inline comment composer and inspect the selected area. Adjust the selection if it includes irrelevant content.
Describe the actual issue and desired result. For example: “This card title wraps into three lines on mobile; keep it to two without reducing the body text size.”
Confirm the intended agent is still selected, then Send. The request includes the visual crop and contextual metadata.
After the agent responds or changes the project, revisit the same page and viewport to verify the result. Send a focused follow-up if the issue remains.
outcome: The agent receives visual evidence together with an actionable instruction. You can inspect the same page while keeping the conversation in project context.
troubleshooting: A screenshot alone does not explain the required change. State what should improve and what should stay unchanged. If you switch chats before sending, recheck the destination; feedback is not permanently tied to the agent that was selected when Review was opened.

title: Create and organize personal tasks
summary: Keep a personal project backlog and turn a clear requirement into agent work.
before: Select the project that owns the work and open Tasks. Personal Board is your local task list; external tracker connections appear as separate sources.
steps: Select Personal Board, then New task. Enter a short outcome-focused Name and a Description that explains the required behavior.
Include enough detail to judge the result. For example, an empty-state task can specify what the user should understand, the action to offer, and the desktop and mobile layouts to check.
Choose Save. The task appears in the board and opens in the main area, where you can review its description.
Use the task header to adjust its status and priority. Keep status aligned with the actual work: creating a task does not mean an agent has started it.
Edit the personal task description directly when requirements change. Changes are saved automatically; give the editor a moment to finish before closing the app.
When the requirement is ready, choose Implement to prepare an agent request. Review the project, configuration, and task details before sending.
outcome: The task remains associated with its project and can be revisited from Personal Board. Work started from it can be traced back through the linked agent.
troubleshooting: If a task appears missing, first check the selected project and source. A task in Personal Board is separate from a ticket in Jira or another external tracker. Keep acceptance criteria in the description instead of relying on a short title. Editing a requirement while an agent is already working may require a direct follow-up to make the new scope clear.

title: Connect an external task source
summary: Connect a project to an external task source so its issues can become context for agent work.
before: Open the intended project and Tasks. You need authorized access to the external tracker and the credentials or environment-variable reference requested by its connection form. Do not paste a token into a task description or agent message.
steps: Use the add-connection action beside the task sources. Choose Jira, Linear, ClickUp, or Asana.
Give the connection a recognizable name. Enter the provider-specific connection details. For Jira, the form includes the site URL, email, and API token.
Choose the relevant board or other source using the form’s source fields and loading controls. Confirm that it belongs to the project you intend to work on.
Set the assignee filter if you want a narrower view. For a provider that supports loading assignees, load the list before choosing a person.
Optionally choose the suggested status when a pull request is done. This is a suggestion shown in the shipping workflow; it does not automatically update the external issue.
Choose Save, select the new source in Tasks, and confirm that the expected issues appear. Open one issue and review its details before starting implementation.
outcome: The external source becomes a project task view. Its issues provide context for agent work while retaining their identity in the original tracker.
troubleshooting: If loading fails, inspect the actual connection error and check the site, credentials, source identifier, and account access. An empty list can also be caused by an assignee filter. Fields differ between providers; use the instructions in the selected provider’s form. The screenshot shows the Jira setup form with no new credentials entered.

title: Start agent work from a task
summary: Prepare an agent request from a task while keeping the work linked to its requirement.
before: Open Tasks in the correct project and select the personal or external task. Read its description, status, and priority before deciding what the agent should implement.
steps: Clarify the expected result in the task. Resolve conflicting requirements and identify any design or reference material the agent needs.
Choose Implement in the task header. Choro opens a new-agent composer with the task context prepared. If the task already has implementation work, the action may be labeled Reimplement.
Read the prepared request. Confirm the task identifier and scope, then add any limits that are specific to this implementation.
Choose the provider, model, effort, access, and working mode. Use Plan if you want to agree on an approach before implementation.
Send the request when it is ready. Follow the linked agent, answer questions, and inspect the actual result against the task.
Return to the task to follow its linked work. Review changed files and relevant checks before treating the requirement as complete.
outcome: The agent conversation carries a reference to the task, so you can move between the requirement and its implementation.
troubleshooting: Opening Implement prepares a draft; it does not itself finish the task or prove the requested behavior works. If the task changes during a run, send a focused follow-up to explain the change. For external tasks, check the live source when details may have changed. Avoid creating several implementation agents for the same requirement unless you intend to coordinate that work.

title: Create and edit a project doc
summary: Write project requirements, plans, and decisions in documents that stay close to the work.
before: Select a project and open Docs. Use a document for information that benefits from more structure than a short task description.
steps: Choose New in the Docs panel. Start with Blank Doc or a suitable template, such as Feature / PRD, Technical Design, Research Spike, or Decision Record.
Give the document a recognizable title. Use the template’s sections as prompts, then replace example or placeholder text with the actual project information.
Write the outcome, scope, and important constraints. For a feature document, include how a reader can tell whether the result is correct.
Use headings and short sections to make the document easy to scan. Keep unresolved questions explicit instead of leaving contradictory instructions in the main requirement.
Return to the document from the Docs list to review it. Use its status and labels to organize it where those controls are available.
For a structure you expect to reuse, open the document’s menu and choose Save as template. Give the template a clear name so it can be selected for a future document.
outcome: The project has a readable source of requirements or decisions that you can revisit and use when preparing agent work.
troubleshooting: A template provides structure; it does not know your project’s requirements. Check that copied text is relevant before handing it to an agent. If Choro reports a saving error, resolve that error before using the document as an implementation source. A saved template is a reusable snapshot, so later edits to the original document are not a reason to assume the template has changed.

title: Start agent work from a doc
summary: Turn a reviewed project document into a linked implementation request.
before: Open the document in Docs and check that it describes a concrete outcome. Resolve important ambiguities and make the scope clear before handing it to an agent.
steps: Choose Implement in the document header. If it already has implementation work, the action may be labeled Reimplement.
Review the new-agent draft. Choro includes the document reference and asks the agent to read it before making changes.
Check the attached document and selected project. Add specific limits or clarification when only part of the document should be implemented.
Choose a provider, model, effort, access level, and working mode. Use Plan when the approach needs review before implementation.
Send the request, then respond to questions or decisions in the agent conversation. The document remains the requirement source for that work.
Compare the result with the document, inspect changed files, and perform the checks that matter for the described behavior. Return to the document to follow its linked implementation.
outcome: The implementation conversation is linked to the project document. The prepared request gives the agent the document path and asks it to clarify ambiguity rather than making broad assumptions.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows a prepared draft, before sending. Opening Implement does not automatically send the request. If you edit the document after work starts, tell the agent what changed and whether it should revise its plan. Reimplement prepares another implementation flow; inspect existing work before starting overlapping agents.

title: Follow the work linked to a task or doc
summary: Move between a requirement and the agent work that was started from it.
before: Open a task in Tasks or a document in Docs. Linked work is most useful when the agent was started through that item’s Implement action.
steps: Look for the linked agent indicator near the task or document header. Open it to inspect the implementation conversation.
Confirm that the conversation refers to the intended requirement. Read the latest response, pending questions, and the reported status.
Inspect the resulting files and behavior. A task’s Done label or an agent’s final message is not a substitute for checking the requested outcome.
Return to the task or document when you need to compare the implementation with the original description. Use its linked design or pull-request indicators when present.
Send corrections in the relevant conversation and keep the requirement up to date when the intended scope changes. If you start another implementation, make the relationship to earlier work explicit.
outcome: You can trace the requirement, implementation conversation, and relevant result without reconstructing the history from unrelated chats.
troubleshooting: If no linked agent is shown, check whether work was started from this exact item or from a separate new-agent request. Similar titles do not prove that two records are linked. A Reimplement action can be available when prior work exists; inspect that work before starting another run. External task statuses and suggested pull-request status changes still need the appropriate review.

title: Change appearance and workspace preferences
summary: Choose a theme, adjust panel styling, and put new conversation activity where you prefer to read it.
before: Open Settings (⌘, by default), then choose Appearance. These preferences control the Choro workspace. They do not change the design of the app or website you are building.
steps: Choose a theme card. Each card previews its own sidebar, canvas, cards, and accent colors; the selected theme shows a checkmark. Try the light theme if you prefer a bright workspace, or select a dark palette that keeps text comfortable to read.
Under Sidebar surface, choose Flat for a uniform panel or Colorful · theme cast for the theme’s accent tint at the top of each sidebar. The tint fades toward the middle of the panel.
Under Divider lines, choose Soft · fades at ends or Solid · edge to edge. This changes the thin boundaries between the sidebars, main area, and header.

Under Conversation layout, choose Classic · newest at bottom if you prefer reading the conversation toward its latest message at the bottom. Choose Top-down · newest first to place the composer first, with the latest conversation growing downward.

Close Settings and return to a conversation. Check text readability and the position of recent activity in your normal window size. Return to Appearance to adjust any choice that feels harder to follow.
outcome: Changes are applied and saved when you select them; there is no separate Save button. You can change each preference independently and return to your previous selection at any time.
troubleshooting: If the running app in Preview still has its original colors, that is expected: a Choro theme changes the workspace around Preview. Changing conversation layout also does not rewrite or remove your messages. If a layout feels unfamiliar, switch back to Classic and compare it in the same conversation. A theme card’s colors may look different from the currently selected workspace because each preview deliberately shows that theme’s own palette.

title: Ask a project question with Quick Ask
summary: Ask a focused project question without starting an implementation agent.
before: Select the project you want to ask about. Quick Ask uses your configured provider; a question can still require provider access even though it does not start a full agent conversation.
steps: Open Quick Ask with Command+Option+A, or your customized Quick Ask shortcut. The panel opens over the current workspace.
Check the scope control below the question. Choose the project for questions about its repository, or General when the question is not about a project.
Check the model control. Quick Ask has its own model preference, so it may differ from the model used for new agents.
Write a focused question. For example: “How do I run and verify this project?” Name the relevant feature or file when that helps disambiguate the request.
Send the question and read the answer. Follow any repository references and compare suggested commands with the actual project documentation before running them.
Ask a follow-up in the same panel if you need clarification. Use Start agent only when you want to turn the discussion into a reviewed agent draft.
outcome: The answer appears in Quick Ask while your workspace remains available. The conversation is recorded in Ask History so you can return to it later.
troubleshooting: Project scope matters: General is not a substitute for checking the intended repository. An answer is guidance, not proof that a command ran or a feature works. In the demo, the follow-up distinguishes a basic file-presence check from a real UI test. If a provider is unavailable, resolve its sign-in or configuration before retrying.

title: Continue a Quick Ask conversation
summary: Continue a Quick Ask discussion or return to it from Ask History.
