before: Use the current panel for an immediate follow-up. To revisit earlier context later, explicitly select the saved conversation in Ask History; a normal fresh Quick Ask launch starts a new session.
steps: After reading an answer, enter a focused follow-up in the same Quick Ask composer. Refer to the specific claim you want clarified, such as what a verification command leaves untested.
Read the new answer alongside the earlier exchange. Keep the same topic in this conversation so the follow-up has a clear reference.
Open Ask History using the book icon in the Quick Ask header. The history view lists saved conversations and shows the selected transcript.
Search by a distinctive question, answer term, or project, then select the conversation you meant to revisit. Confirm its project and opening question before continuing.
Use the “Continue this conversation…” composer beneath the saved transcript to add a follow-up. Read the resulting answer in that conversation.
Choose New Question when you want a separate topic, or Start Agent when the discussion should become an actionable project request.
outcome: The saved discussion retains its related questions and answers. You can revisit the reasoning without assuming every old conversation is automatically included in new Quick Ask context.
troubleshooting: If an earlier answer seems missing, check Ask History and the selected conversation before asking the same question again. A new session and a follow-up have different context. Verify older advice against the current repository because files and requirements may have changed since the answer was recorded.

title: Turn a Quick Ask answer into an agent task
summary: Move a useful Quick Ask discussion into an agent draft you can review before sending.
before: Have a Quick Ask answer or saved conversation ready, and make sure the intended project has been added to Choro. Decide what concrete work should follow from the discussion.
steps: Read the answer and identify the desired action. Separate the answer’s suggestions from the work you actually want done.
Choose Start agent in Quick Ask or Start Agent in the selected Ask History conversation. If a project choice is offered, select the repository where the work belongs.
Review the prepared new-agent draft. It carries Quick Ask context into the request; the history handoff includes the saved transcript.
Confirm the project below the composer and review the model, effort, and access controls. The new agent configuration can differ from the Quick Ask model.
Add a clear instruction describing the next outcome and its limits. Ask the agent to verify any claims from the earlier answer against the repository before relying on them.
Use Plan when the approach needs discussion, then send the draft when ready. Follow the resulting agent conversation and review its actual changes and checks.
outcome: The discussion becomes context for a separate agent request. Opening Start agent prepares a draft; it does not automatically submit implementation work.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the unsent history handoff. Do not treat a pasted answer as evidence that its suggested actions already happened. If no project is available, add one before starting the agent. For a broad discussion, narrow the requested outcome so the agent does not interpret every suggestion as a requirement.

title: Create and use a Riff
summary: Save reusable instructions as a Riff and select them in an agent request.
before: Use a Riff for a repeatable way of working, such as reviewing acceptance criteria. Keep the specific task in the request instead of baking one project’s temporary requirement into the reusable instructions.
steps: Open Settings → Skills → Choro Riffs and choose New Riff.
Enter a recognizable Name and a short Description. The description helps you identify the Riff in the slash menu.
Write the full workflow in Instructions. For a review Riff, specify what to inspect, how to report gaps, and whether it should change files.
If you use Generate with AI, first provide the name and description, then review the generated instructions before saving.
Choose Save Riff. Confirm that it appears in the list and is Enabled.
Return to an agent composer, type a slash followed by the Riff name, and choose the entry labeled Riff. The selected Riff appears as a chip; its instructions are kept out of the visible request text.
Add the actual task and any relevant references, review the configuration, and send when ready. Return to Settings to edit the Riff when the reusable workflow changes.
outcome: The saved Riff is available across projects and supplies reusable guidance when selected. The request still needs to explain the specific outcome you want.
troubleshooting: The demo’s Acceptance Check Riff asks for a comparison against requirements and a report of remaining checks. A Riff supplies instructions; it does not change the agent’s provider permissions or guarantee that its checks pass. If it is missing from the slash menu, check its name and Enabled state. Bandmates can also link Riffs through their Skills configuration.

title: Inspect an agent’s changed files
summary: Inspect the actual edits behind an agent’s result before deciding what to keep.
before: Use the completed conversation for the task you want to review. Changes shown in the project Git panel can include other work, so distinguish the agent’s Files changed card from the whole repository.
steps: Read the final response and note what the agent says it changed, what it checked, and any unfinished work.
Find Files changed in the conversation. Check the filenames and addition/deletion counts against the requested scope.
Choose Open diff to inspect the changes together, or open a particular file from the card.
Read the removed and added lines with their surrounding context. In the demo, the only implementation edit adds aria-label="Main navigation" to the existing nav element.
Use Open File when you need more surrounding code. Check behavior in Preview or your usual runtime as well; a plausible diff is not a functional test.
If the result is wrong, return to the conversation with a focused correction. Describe the expected behavior and the relevant file rather than asking for an unspecified rewrite.
outcome: You can explain what changed and whether it matches the intended task before committing or shipping it.
troubleshooting: The demo Git panel also contains an unrelated untracked notes file. Its presence does not mean this agent created it. Review file provenance and selection before delivery. An empty Files changed card can be valid for read-only work; a completed response alone is not proof of an implementation.

title: Use the What to check checklist
summary: Use the generated checklist to perform the manual checks that still matter.
before: What to check is generated after relevant file changes. It is a review aid, not evidence that the actions have already been performed.
steps: Open the completed implementation conversation and find What to check below the result and changed files.
Expand the checklist if it is collapsed. Read each action and its expected result, including any additional detail shown for the item.
Perform the described journey in the running app with the required setup. For an accessibility check, use a screen reader or accessibility inspector instead of guessing from the visual layout.
Check an item only after observing its expected result. Leave a failed or unperformed check unchecked.
When a check fails, tell the agent the action, observed result, expected result, and relevant context. Review its correction and repeat that check.
Review the count at the top of the card before delivery. Also consider requirements outside the suggested checklist if the task has additional risks.
outcome: The checklist records which suggested manual checks you actually completed. In the screenshot, 0 of 1 checked means the accessibility journey still needs human verification.
troubleshooting: Preparing checks means generation is still running; Couldn’t prepare checks offers Retry. No manual checks suggested is not a guarantee that the software is correct. A checkmark is your review record, not a replacement for tests, code review, or checking the original requirements.

title: Run Code Review and resolve findings
summary: Ask for a code review, read its coverage, and resolve actionable findings.
before: Finish the implementation turn and inspect its changed files first. Code Review is another agent pass; it can take time and provider resources.
steps: Open the implementation conversation and choose Code review near the composer. The conversation shows Sent for code review and a Reviewing activity while the pass runs.
Read the resulting Code review card. Check Coverage to understand which files were inspected and any limitations.
If findings are present, read the issue, what happens, and suggested fix. Open referenced code and decide which findings apply to the intended behavior.
Select the findings you want addressed and choose Fix selected, or use Fix all when all pending findings should be addressed.
Inspect the resulting edits and repeat relevant checks. A request to fix findings starts more work; it does not immediately prove those findings are resolved.
If the result says No findings, still read its coverage and complete any remaining manual checks before delivery.
outcome: You have a review result tied to the conversation’s changed code and a deliberate response to any findings.
troubleshooting: The demo review inspected one file and explicitly ran no tests or commands during its read-only review. No findings means no issues were reported within that review’s coverage. Coverage not confirmed is a different result and should not be treated as a clean review. Use tests and runtime checks alongside this feedback.

title: Coding provider unavailable or signed out
summary: Identify whether a provider problem comes from installation, authentication, or the selected model.
before: Read the exact error in the failed conversation and note which provider it used. New agents, Quick Ask, and quick generation can use different defaults.
steps: Check the provider and model in the affected composer. Confirm you are troubleshooting the provider that actually failed.
If the provider is not installed or asks for sign-in, complete its supported local setup or sign-in flow. Changing a model does not create account access.
Open Settings → AI generation and check the default for the affected feature. Compare it with the override shown in the current conversation.
Try a small read-only question after completing setup. Confirm that a real response arrives before restarting a large task.
If the error names a missing model, tool, or permission, address that specific cause. Full access does not supply credentials or an unavailable model.
If it still fails, record the provider, model, exact error, and time for a support report. Remove tokens and private request content before sharing.
outcome: You can retry with a working provider configuration or report a specific unresolved failure.
troubleshooting: A successful request through one provider does not prove another provider is authenticated. Repeated retries with unchanged credentials usually repeat the same failure. Follow your provider’s current setup guidance for installation and login.

title: An agent is stuck, interrupted, or failing
summary: Determine whether an agent needs a decision, has stopped, or has encountered an error.
before: Keep the original conversation and partial files available. A stalled-looking workflow status alone is not enough to diagnose a provider failure.
steps: Read the latest message and live activity. Distinguish Working or Reviewing from a saved In progress workflow label.
Look for a question, plan decision, or permission card. Answer the specific card instead of repeatedly sending Continue.
If the provider reports an error, record its wording and check whether it concerns authentication, access, a tool, or the project path.
Use Stop when you intentionally need to interrupt active work. Inspect partial changes before starting another agent on the same files.
After correcting the cause, resume the saved conversation when that action is available, or send a precise follow-up explaining what should continue.
Review the next response and its files. If recovery fails, report the original error and recovery attempt rather than creating repeated duplicate tasks.
outcome: You either unblock the original work or preserve enough evidence for a useful diagnosis.
troubleshooting: Stopping is not a rollback. A completed provider turn can leave manual checks, integration work, or a workflow status unfinished. For delegated work, inspect the lead and assignment separately.

title: A Bandmate cannot start or resume
summary: Find why a delegated assignment cannot begin or continue.
before: Open the lead that owns the assignment. Keep the failed assignment and its report so you can distinguish a new failure from an earlier attempt.
steps: Open Band and select the affected assignment. Read its brief, current state, and latest provider error.
Check whether it is waiting on another assignment or a concurrency limit. Waiting for a dependency is different from a failed launch.
For a saved Bandmate, check Settings → Band: the profile must be enabled and its provider configuration must be usable.
For a permission or MCP startup error, inspect the named policy or tool. Increasing concurrency will not repair an authentication or permission failure.
Correct the identified cause, then use the explicit Resume action for stopped work when available. Opening the panel alone does not resume it.
Read the resumed activity and the lead’s integration result. Ask for a bounded revision if the specialist completed only part of the brief.
outcome: You can distinguish scheduling, profile configuration, provider errors, and explicit pauses before retrying.
troubleshooting: Turning Delegation off prevents new runs but is not the control for stopping an existing team. Do not broaden access solely to silence an unexplained error. A failed assignment is not successful integration, even if another Bandmate finished.

title: A project or file cannot be accessed
summary: Check project scope and file access before assuming work has disappeared.
before: Know the folder or file you expected to open. Sidebar entries and search results are navigation aids; the underlying file may have moved or become unavailable.
steps: Confirm the active project name and any Solo scope in the workspace. A different project can legitimately show a different file tree.
Open Code and inspect the project tree. Check whether you added the repository root, a parent folder, or a nested subproject.
If search returns nothing, shorten the query and inspect its Files, Chats, Tasks, or Docs filter. Search does not include every generated directory.
If the folder is on a disconnected drive or was moved, make the correct location available and open that project folder again.
If macOS reports an access denial, review Choro’s permission for that folder and retry the specific read. Do not remove the project files as a troubleshooting step.
Report the action, expected file, exact error, and whether direct file access works if the problem remains. Avoid including private file contents unnecessarily.
outcome: You identify a scope, location, indexing, or permission problem without discarding the original work.
troubleshooting: A missing sidebar tool can be enabled through Manage. Removing a favorite changes navigation placement; it does not delete repository files. Assets that point to local files still need their sources to remain available.

title: A script fails or Preview will not load
summary: Use terminal evidence to diagnose a failed script or an unavailable Preview.
before: Identify the saved script and the URL you intended to open. A terminal reporting success does not necessarily mean a web server is still running.
steps: Open the terminal for the script and read its last output, exit status, and any reported URL or port.
Check the saved command through Run → Edit scripts. Confirm it is appropriate for this repository and that the required dependencies are installed.
For a stopped service, correct the error before using Restart. A normal verification script may exit successfully because it is not a long-running server.
For a port-in-use error, identify the process that owns the port or choose a suitable free port. Do not repeatedly launch duplicate instances.
When the service is running, open Preview with the actual URL it reports. Check the protocol, hostname, and port rather than copying a generic example.
If the URL works externally but not in Preview, record both results and the displayed error. Preserve useful terminal output for the support report.
outcome: You can separate command failure, normal process exit, port conflicts, and preview-specific problems.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows a deliberately stopped demo server and its restart controls. KeyboardInterrupt after Control+C can be expected. For a static HTML file, a development server may not be necessary; use the local-file preview workflow when appropriate.

title: A task source will not connect or refresh
summary: Check the connected source and its errors before creating duplicate task connections.
before: Use the account and project that should contain the tasks. An empty filtered board is different from a failed connection.
steps: Open Tasks and identify the selected source. Personal tasks do not require an external tracker connection.
If setup is incomplete, open the source configuration and review its required fields. Use the tracker’s actual account and project details.
For authentication or permission errors, check that the connected account still has access to the intended tracker project.
If connection succeeds but tasks seem missing, clear restrictive board filters and verify the selected project or source.
Retry refresh after addressing the cause, then check whether the expected task appears. Read any new error instead of assuming the old failure still applies.
If the issue persists, report the tracker type, failed action, time, and redacted error. Keep passwords, tokens, and private task content out of the report.
outcome: You identify whether the issue is setup, account access, filtering, or refresh rather than silently duplicating sources.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the connection form, not proof of a successful external login. Do not enter a different account’s credentials merely to make the board populate. Existing task links may refer to a different source than the currently selected board.

title: Voice input is not working
summary: Check voice readiness and microphone access when speech is not becoming usable input.
before: Keep a text-input route available while troubleshooting. Distinguish microphone capture, speech recognition, and a provider’s response; they can fail independently.
steps: Open Settings → Voice and inspect the setup and readiness state. Complete any required local voice setup before retrying.
Confirm that the Mac can receive audio from the microphone you intend to use. Check system microphone permission for Choro if access was denied.
Try a short, clear phrase in the intended voice flow and observe whether text appears. Avoid sending a long task while testing capture.
Read and correct the transcription before submitting an implementation request. Speech recognition can mishear filenames and commands.
If transcription appears but no answer follows, inspect the conversation’s provider configuration and error separately from microphone capture.
Report which stage failed, the readiness state, and any exact error if the problem persists. Avoid including sensitive recorded speech in a diagnostic report.
outcome: You can identify whether setup, capture, transcription, or the downstream provider needs attention.
troubleshooting: A working keyboard composer does not prove microphone access is granted. Project Talk and dictated agent requests serve different purposes; confirm the intended conversation before sending transcribed instructions.

title: Choose a design workflow: Studio or Figma
summary: Choose the design workflow that matches the source you want to create or use.
before: Open a project and enable Design through Manage if it is not visible. Studio creates local designs; Figma links provide external references.
steps: Open Design and choose New Design to see the available workflows.

Choose Studio for a project-local design with screens, a visual editor, and a design agent. You can begin without connecting a separate design account; the agent still needs a working coding provider.
Choose Figma when you want to add an existing design link as a reference. Keep the source accessible to the people and tools that will use it.
Before implementation, state which design or screens are authoritative and which behavior the agent should build. Review the implementation against that source.
outcome: You start in a workflow whose storage, connection requirements, and handoff match the task.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the New Design menu in the demo. A saved Figma URL is not a claim that Choro can edit that file or that the coding agent has Figma tool access. Studio generation and implementation are separate stages: refining a design does not automatically change your application code.

title: Add and organize screens
summary: Organize a Studio design into named screens that are easy to review and hand off.
before: Open a Studio design and finish any unsaved edit before changing its screen structure. Wait for an active design-agent pass to finish before reorganizing the same screens.
steps: Open Screens to see the design’s screen list. Choose All screens for an overview of the available layouts.
Use the plus beside Screens to add a screen. Replace the suggested name with the screen’s purpose, then save.
Open a screen’s three-dot menu and choose Rename when its purpose changes. Use Duplicate to explore a variation while retaining the original.
Use Move up or Move down to put screens in a useful review order, such as overview, list, then detail.
Use Archive / restore to manage screens you do not currently want in the active set. Review archived screens before assuming they were deleted.
Open each active screen and inspect its content. Use Screen actions → Refresh previews if the overview thumbnail appears out of date.
Before implementation, select the screens that belong in the requested scope instead of assuming every exploratory variation should be built.
outcome: The design has a clear active screen set and a predictable review order.
troubleshooting: The demo screen menu exposes naming, duplication, ordering, archive, and viewport actions. Archive is different from deleting the design. A thumbnail is a preview; inspect the full screen before judging small text or responsive behavior.

title: Edit text and styles with the visual inspector
summary: Make focused content and style edits directly in a Studio screen.
before: Open a saved Studio screen and wait for any design-agent pass touching it to finish. Decide which element should change before editing.
steps: Choose Edit in the screen toolbar. Click the actual element on the canvas; the selection outline and inspector identify what you selected.
For a heading, open Content and edit its Text. Check the heading size separately from the words so the semantic hierarchy remains appropriate.
Open Style for visual properties available for the selected element. Make one focused change at a time and inspect its effect on surrounding content.
Use Advanced or the general fields only when you intend to change attributes such as an ID or class. Such changes may affect styling or references.
Move focus away from the edited field and watch the save status. Wait for Saved before switching screens or handing the design to an implementation agent.
Use Undo or Redo for a recent editor change when appropriate, then inspect the result. Switch to Preview to assess the screen without the editing outline.
outcome: The selected screen contains the intended edit, with a confirmed save state.
troubleshooting: No selected element means the inspector has no editing target. Clicking a container instead of its child can expose different controls. A local style change may override a design-system value, so check the design’s overrides if a later system update appears ineffective.

title: Preview desktop and mobile layouts
summary: Check how a Studio screen responds to desktop and mobile viewport sizes.
before: Use a saved screen whose content is ready to inspect. Changing viewport size exposes layout behavior; it does not automatically redesign a layout that is not responsive.
steps: Open Screens and use the screen’s three-dot menu. Choose Mobile viewport to inspect the narrower layout or Desktop viewport to return to the wider layout.
Open the screen and choose Preview. Inspect text wrapping, navigation, controls, and the order of content at the selected viewport.
Scroll through the entire screen. Check for clipped content, horizontal overflow, overlapping controls, and important actions pushed out of reach.
Use Zoom to make the canvas comfortable to inspect. Zoom changes your view; the screen’s viewport choice determines its layout size.
Return to Edit or ask the design agent for a focused correction if the mobile layout needs different spacing, stacking, or navigation.
Repeat the check at the other viewport after each significant correction. Review the actual implemented app at relevant sizes later as a separate step.
outcome: You have inspected the design at both viewport sizes and can describe any remaining responsive issues.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the viewport choices in a real Studio screen menu. A desktop thumbnail alone cannot establish mobile readiness. A static design preview also does not prove that the eventual app’s navigation, data loading, or form submission works.

title: Studio changes are not appearing or saving
summary: Separate an unsaved screen edit from a stale preview or a failed design-agent change.
before: Keep the current editor and error available until you know whether the latest edit was saved. Avoid editing the same screen simultaneously from the inspector and an active design-agent pass.
steps: Read the editor’s save status. Saved indicates the editor has completed its save; a pending or failed state needs attention before you navigate away.
If Retry save is offered, correct the reported issue and retry. If Keep draft & reload is offered for recovery, preserve the draft before reconciling it with the current screen.
When the full screen is correct but its overview thumbnail is stale, use Screens → Screen actions → Refresh previews.
If an agent reports that a transaction was rejected, read its follow-up and inspect the actual screen. A rejected attempt is not proof that the proposed changes were applied.
For a design-system change, check whether you only edited a draft. Review changes and explicitly apply the intended system version before expecting bound designs to use it.
If a system update is applied but an element looks unchanged, check local overrides and hardcoded styles. They can intentionally take precedence.
Report the design, screen, action, exact error, and whether the editor said Saved if the issue persists. Keep any recoverable draft until the discrepancy is understood.
outcome: You know whether to finish saving, refresh a preview, recover a draft, or review a system change.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the Saved indicator and a selected element in the visual inspector. It is an orientation image, not a simulated error. Refreshing a thumbnail does not repair an unsaved document, and repeatedly restarting the agent can make the original failure harder to diagnose.

title: Create your first Studio design
summary: Create a Studio design and develop its first screens with a design agent.
before: Add the intended project and make sure a coding provider is usable. Studio can begin without a separately connected design account.
steps: Open Design → New Design → Studio. Replace the suggested name with a clear description of the work.
Choose an available applied design system if you have one, or begin without a system. You can review a system choice later.
Save the new design, then open Agent. Check the model and access controls before sending a request.
Describe the audience, screens, content, visual direction, and important states. For example: “Create an onboarding overview, project list, and project detail for a client portal.”
Let the design pass finish, then inspect All screens and open each screen. Compare the actual layouts with the requested content and behavior.
Ask for a focused refinement when a screen misses a requirement. Use the visual inspector for small text or style edits, and confirm that edits are saved.
Use Implement only when you are ready to prepare a separate coding-agent request. Review that request before sending it.
outcome: You have a saved Studio design with screens you can inspect, refine, and hand off for implementation.
troubleshooting: The demo overview shows three screens created in Studio. A design agent’s summary is not a substitute for inspecting those screens. Keep content fictional for demos, and distinguish a design prototype from working application behavior.

title: Refine a design with an agent
summary: Ask the Studio agent for a precise design change while preserving the parts you already approve.
before: Open the intended design and finish any unsaved visual edit. Select the screen you want to discuss, or All screens for a request that spans the design.
steps: Open Agent and check the scope shown above the conversation. Confirm the design and screen before sending a request.
Describe the observed problem and the expected result. For example: “On Overview, make the upcoming review date easier to find while keeping the navigation and palette.”
Name what should remain unchanged. For a change across screens, explicitly identify the shared pattern and affected screens.
Review the chosen model and access configuration, then start the request. Let the current pass finish before starting another edit to the same screen.
Read the response, including any rejected transaction or limitation, and inspect the actual screen changes.
Check the relevant desktop and mobile layouts. Send a focused follow-up if the result still misses the requirement.
Prepare implementation only after the design itself is ready. Studio refinement does not automatically update application code.
outcome: The design changes in a bounded, reviewable way, with the conversation retaining the reason for the change.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows a completed design pass and its three-screen result. Check the screens yourself instead of treating the agent’s review claim as proof of every interaction or accessibility requirement. If a pass fails, preserve its error and inspect which changes actually saved.

title: Manage design conversations and history
summary: Keep separate Studio conversations for different design questions without losing previous discussions.
before: Open the Studio design whose discussion you want. Design conversation history belongs to that design; it is separate from the implementation agent’s conversation.
steps: Open Agent and use the conversation picker above the messages to see previous design conversations.
Select a conversation to read its request, progress, and result. Check the design and selected screen before continuing it.
Use the plus beside the picker to create a new conversation for a separate design question.
Describe the new scope explicitly. A fresh conversation still works on the current design; it does not create an independent copy of its screens.
Return to the picker to revisit earlier decisions. Wait for an active pass to finish before switching when the control is unavailable.
For an actual saved-edit rollback, inspect the Undo saved edit and Redo saved edit actions under Screen actions. Conversation selection itself does not roll the design back.
outcome: You can revisit earlier reasoning and keep new design discussions focused while understanding that they share the current design.
troubleshooting: The demo picker contains a completed generation conversation and New agent 2. Selecting the older conversation opens its messages, not a historical version of the canvas. If you want a visual alternative, duplicate a screen and name the variation before asking for changes.

title: Implement a design or selected screens
summary: Prepare an implementation request from a saved Studio design or a deliberate screen selection.
before: Finish the design edits you want included and confirm their save state. Decide whether the task should build the whole design or only particular screens.
steps: For the whole design, choose Implement in its header. For a subset, open Screens → Screen actions → Implement selected screens.
In the selection dialog, keep only the screens that belong in this implementation and choose Implement selected.
Review the prepared agent draft. It points the agent to an immutable Studio handoff containing the selected design snapshot, tokens, assets, and screens.
Add the functional requirements that the design alone cannot establish, such as navigation, validation, data loading, and empty or error states.
Confirm the project, provider, model, access, and any Solo choice before sending the request. The handoff draft is not submitted merely by opening it.
Follow the implementation conversation, inspect its changed files, and run the actual app. Compare the result with the handed-off screens and the functional requirements.
If you change the Studio design later, prepare a new handoff when the implementation should use that newer version. Explain the intended update rather than assuming the earlier snapshot changed.
outcome: The coding agent receives a specific design snapshot and a clear implementation scope that you can review against the result.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the screen-selection dialog. Design data and prototype interactions are illustrative; production behavior still needs implementation and verification. Studio source design files should remain intact unless modifying them is explicitly part of the task.

title: Use the process monitor
summary: See how Choro and its related processes are using memory and CPU.
before: Open the monitor while the workload you want to investigate is present. Record what is running so a resource reading has useful context.
steps: Open Settings → Process monitor and read the Choro, Related, and CPU summary.
Read the measurement note below the summary. Physical footprint includes compressed and swapped memory; a fallback resident-memory reading is a different measurement.
Inspect Inside Choro to see the allocation types contributing to the application’s own memory.
Scroll through Related processes. Choro groups them by project and agent when ownership can be identified, with larger groups first.
Use Refresh to take another snapshot after the activity changes. Compare like-for-like workloads rather than treating one temporary peak as a leak.
If you need to stop work, return to its conversation, terminal, or service controls and stop the intended task there. Then refresh the monitor to observe the effect.
For a performance report, include the workload, approximate duration, memory and CPU readings, and whether the usage settles after the work finishes.
outcome: You can distinguish the app’s own resource use from related agents, web content, terminals, and scripts.
troubleshooting: The screenshot is one live demo reading, not a recommended limit or a performance benchmark. Unidentified ownership does not prove a process is unrelated. A high value during active generation needs different interpretation from steady growth while idle.

title: Understand where Choro stores data and what providers receive
summary: Understand the difference between local workspace storage, project files, and provider processing.
before: Treat project content, conversation context, and exported archives as potentially sensitive. The exact data sent to a coding provider depends on the task, selected tools, and that provider’s configuration.
steps: Keep your repository backup separate from Choro’s workspace backup. Adding a project points Choro at a local folder; a workspace export is not a full copy of every repository on disk.
Use Settings → Data & backups to export the supported workspace archive. Retain the resulting file securely and review the import guide before restoring it.

Expect Choro preferences and workspace records in its application data directory. The standard Mac location is under ~/Library/Application Support/com.ritmus.choro; isolated demo or development builds can use a different data root.
Before sending a request, review its attachments, references, and scope. Coding providers can receive prompts and the file or tool context used to carry out that request.

For Voice, distinguish audio from text. Choro’s voice settings describe audio as processed on the Mac and not retained; text used in Project Talk or an agent request can still be processed by the selected coding provider.

Review local transcript retention in Voice settings and check the provider’s own policies for its processing and retention. Local audio processing does not mean every downstream text operation stays on the Mac.

When sharing diagnostics, include the smallest useful evidence. Keep secrets, unrelated private files, and complete workspace archives out of public reports unless you deliberately intend to share them.
outcome: You can make informed choices about backups, request context, and what to share with a provider or support.
troubleshooting: Use the app’s supported export/import flow instead of editing its state database directly. Import replaces supported workspace state and may require a restart; it is not a routine way to repair an unrelated provider error. This guide describes product behavior, not a substitute for the selected provider’s current data policy.

title: Report a problem with useful diagnostic details
summary: Prepare a concise report that makes a Choro problem reproducible.
before: Keep the original error or failed conversation available. Use a small example that demonstrates the issue without including unrelated private work.
steps: Write a short title naming the failed action, such as “Preview stays blank after the server starts.”
Describe the steps from a known starting point. Include the relevant project scope, tool, provider, and whether Solo or Band was involved.
State the expected result and the actual result separately. Copy the exact error text and note when it occurred.
Attach a focused screenshot or relevant terminal excerpt when it clarifies the problem. Remove secrets, personal content, and unrelated information first.
Include the Choro build and macOS version when available, whether the issue repeats, and any recovery steps already tried.
For performance issues, use Settings → Process monitor and report the workload alongside the readings. For provider failures, name the provider and model rather than sharing credentials.

Use the support or feedback route available to you. Choro’s Help → Send feedback opens the requests portal; describe a reproducible problem clearly and follow any portal guidance about the appropriate category.
outcome: The report contains enough evidence to investigate the behavior without requiring someone to guess the missing steps.
troubleshooting: A screenshot of an error without its trigger is often insufficient. Do not publish a complete workspace archive, credential, or private conversation merely because it might contain useful evidence. Preserve the original work until the failure is understood.

title: Request a feature and follow the roadmap
summary: Share a feature request and follow published roadmap progress.
before: Have a concrete problem or workflow in mind. Sign in to the Choro portal when it asks you to identify yourself before submitting a request.
steps: Open Help → Send feedback in Choro, or visit https://choro.usergist.com/choro/requests.
Search existing requests for the same need. Open a relevant request and add useful context or support through the controls offered there instead of creating an unnecessary duplicate.
For a new request, describe the problem, who encounters it, and the outcome that would help. Include a short example of the current workflow.
Keep one main need per request and avoid including credentials or private project information. Submit through the signed-in portal flow.
Open Help → Roadmap, or visit https://choro.usergist.com/choro/roadmap, to see the published roadmap items and their current statuses.
Read the item’s details and updates. Use shipped announcements and help articles to learn how an available feature works.
outcome: Your request has a clear use case, and you know where to follow the product’s published progress.
troubleshooting: A roadmap status is a progress signal, not a guaranteed delivery date or a promise that every requested variation is included. The screenshot shows the desktop menu routes; submitting a request happens in the portal.

title: Create a reusable design system
summary: Create a reusable visual system for Studio designs in your project.
before: Decide whether the system should reflect an existing product or a new direction. If the repository contains several apps, identify which app supplies the source styles.
steps: Open Design → Design systems → New system.
Enter a clear Name and Platform. In the starting-point field, name the relevant app folder or describe the intended visual direction.
Choose Create system. Read the resulting workspace: the starting point is a request, not yet verified evidence of existing product styles.
Use Build with agent to develop the draft. Ask it to distinguish discovered values from proposals and to cover semantic colors, typography, spacing, and reusable component patterns.
Inspect the generated specimen and Library. Review source notes and decisions, and ask for corrections where the draft does not match the intended product.
Choose Review changes to inspect the proposed result and its impact. Apply the system only after reviewing it.
Open an individual Studio design and choose the applied system through its Design system controls. Creating a system does not automatically bind every design to it.
outcome: You have an applied, reusable system that can be selected by the relevant Studio designs.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows a generated draft specimen and its agent summary. Draft and applied versions are distinct. A system created from a request should not be described as extracted from code unless its source evidence supports that claim.

title: Review and apply design-system changes
summary: Review a design-system draft before making it available to linked Studio designs.
before: Finish the system edit or agent pass first. Know which designs already use the system so you can assess the scope of the update.
steps: Open the system workspace and inspect its draft specimen, tokens, typography, and component recipes.
Choose Review changes and wait for the before-and-after previews to finish preparing.
Compare the previews and read the changed values. Review the listed affected designs; the dialog explicitly says when no designs use the system yet.
Check that the update improves the intended shared language without disrupting unrelated screens. Local overrides remain in place and can affect the visible outcome.
Choose Keep editing when the draft needs more work, or Apply system when the reviewed changes are ready.
Open affected designs and inspect representative screens after applying. Check text wrapping, contrast, spacing, and controls at relevant viewport sizes.
outcome: The applied version reflects an explicit review, and you understand which linked designs inherit the update.
troubleshooting: The demo’s first application lists no linked designs, so applying it makes the system available without changing the existing onboarding design. If the system changes while a comparison is open, reopen the review instead of relying on a stale comparison. Applying design tokens does not update already shipped application code.

title: Change a design’s system and manage local overrides
summary: Choose a shared system while understanding the values that remain specific to one Studio design.
before: Open the design you want to change and finish saving any screen edit. Apply a system draft through its own Review changes flow before trying to use it here.
steps: Open the design’s Design system tab and read the currently selected system.
Open the selector and choose the intended applied system. Review the comparison before confirming Use system.
Read the changed tokens and any missing-reference message. Resolve required token mappings before applying a switch that cannot preserve referenced values.
Inspect Local overrides below the selector. These values affect this design and remain in place when the shared system changes.
Use the plus to add an intentional local override, or open an existing value to edit it. Keep exceptions limited and named so later differences are understandable.
Open representative screens and inspect their appearance after the change. Check both system-driven values and hardcoded styles that may be unaffected.
If a change should be shared by every linked design, edit and review the shared system instead of repeating the same local override in each design.
outcome: The design uses a deliberate shared system while retaining only the local differences you intend.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows a real design with no system selected and several local overrides. Selecting a system does not erase these values or rewrite hardcoded screen styles. A draft system must be reviewed and applied before it is available for normal use.

title: Review the implementation against the design
summary: Compare the running implementation with its Studio handoff and functional requirements.
before: Have the completed implementation conversation, the saved Studio design, and a running local app available. An agent finishing does not establish that every screen or interaction is correct.
steps: Read the implementation result and inspect its changed files. Confirm that the edits match the intended screens and do not include unrelated work.
Run the project’s normal development script and open its actual URL in Preview.
Compare each implemented screen with the corresponding Studio screen. Check hierarchy, content, spacing, typography, colors, and the important states described in the task.
Use the app’s real controls: navigate between screens, submit or validate forms where relevant, and check loading, empty, and error behavior. A visual match alone does not verify these actions.
Check relevant desktop and mobile widths and keyboard navigation. Use the What to check checklist to track checks you actually perform.

Send focused feedback to the implementation conversation when you find a mismatch. Include the screen, action, observed result, and expected result; use visual feedback when it clarifies the location.
Recheck the corrected behavior, then review and ship through your normal Git workflow. If the source design changed after the handoff, prepare a new snapshot and explain the intended update.
outcome: You have reviewed both the visual translation and the actual behavior, with remaining manual checks visible.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the implemented Northstar app in Preview beside its unchecked checklist. The screenshot itself does not prove every checklist item passed. Design prototypes can use illustrative data; confirm the intended real behavior separately.

title: Create a design from a task or doc
summary: Use a written task or doc as the starting point for a connected design workflow.
before: Write the requirements first and configure the connected Design workflow in Settings → Design. The task/doc Design action uses that connected workflow; it is separate from creating a local Studio design.
steps: Open the task or doc in the intended project and review its title, description, user journey, and acceptance criteria.
Add missing screens and important states to the written requirements. State what is in scope and what should remain unchanged.
Choose Design in the item’s header. If the action is unavailable, finish the Design connection setup before retrying.
Follow the created design and its assistant. Review how the written requirements were translated into screens and interactions.
Ask for corrections when the design invents behavior or misses a requirement. Keep the source task or doc current when you deliberately change the scope.
Review the finished design before starting implementation. The Design action and Implement action serve different stages of the work.

If you prefer local Studio, create a Studio design from the Design hub and include the relevant requirements in its design-agent request. Do not assume the connected task/doc action creates a Studio file.
outcome: The written requirements guide the design, and you can compare its result with the original task or document.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows a demo doc with Design and Reimplement actions. It demonstrates the entry point, not a completed external design connection. A provider login for coding does not by itself authorize access to a separate design service.

title: Filter an external task board
summary: Narrow a connected task board to the assignee whose work you want to see.
before: Use a configured external task connection with access to its board. Personal Board tasks do not use this external assignee filter.
steps: Open Tasks in the intended project and select the external board tab.
Open Task Connections from the settings control and open the connection you want to adjust.
Check the board and connection before changing Show tasks for. Use Load Users to retrieve the available assignees through that connection.
Select the intended user from the loaded list, or choose All to show all assignees available through the board.
Save the connection, return to its board, and refresh if needed. Check that the cards now match the chosen scope.
If a task is missing, confirm its board membership and assignee in the source tracker. Clear the assignee filter to distinguish filtering from a connection problem.
outcome: The external board displays the intended assignee scope without changing who owns the source issues.
troubleshooting: The screenshot uses unsaved example connection details and shows All assignees. Load Users needs valid connection access; a blank or failed user list is not evidence that the board has no tasks. Filtering changes what Choro displays, not the source tracker’s issue assignments.

title: Understand Orbit and its built-in views
summary: Use Orbit for project environment, detected integrations, and reusable structured records.
before: Open the project whose information you want. Orbit’s built-in views and custom modules serve different purposes.
steps: If Orbit is absent from the project rail, open Manage and enable Orbit.
Open Orbit → Environment to inspect the environment files found in the project. Values begin hidden; choose the correct file before editing.
Open Integrations to inspect services recognized from dependencies and configuration. Detection is a starting point for investigation, not a connection health test.
Open Settings → Orbit to see the fixed built-ins and reusable module definitions. Create a module when a repeatable set of fields is more useful than a free-form doc.
Return to the project’s Orbit and use Add to enable the module there. Creating its definition alone does not add it to every project.
Create records in the project’s module or select its slash command in an agent request. Review both record updates and any code changes the agent makes.
outcome: You can distinguish discovered project configuration from the structured information you deliberately maintain in custom modules.
troubleshooting: The Settings screenshot shows Environment and Integrations as built-ins. Their structure is fixed. Custom module definitions are reusable, while records belong to the project where the module is used. A module is not automatically a live connection to an external analytics service.

title: Find and edit environment variables
summary: Find and update a project’s environment values through Orbit.
before: Know which environment file your application actually loads. Similar names across root and nested app folders can refer to different runtimes.
steps: Open Orbit → Environment and choose the relevant file tab, such as .env or .env.example.
Use Search variables to narrow the list. Use All, Set, or Empty to distinguish configured values from blank entries.
Keep values hidden while sharing your screen. Reveal them only when you need to inspect the contents privately.
Choose Edit on the intended variable and enter the new value. Save to write it to that file, or Cancel to leave it unchanged.
Use Rescan after changes made elsewhere, then confirm the intended key and file reflect the update.
Restart the relevant local service if it reads environment variables only at startup. Verify the resulting behavior in the actual app.
outcome: The intended local environment file contains your change, and you have checked whether the running service uses it.
troubleshooting: Set means the value is nonempty; it does not establish that a credential is valid. Editing .env.example does not necessarily configure the running app. If a save does not appear, check file permissions and rescan. Do not copy secret values into public screenshots or commits.

title: Inspect detected services and integrations
summary: Use Orbit’s detected integrations to understand a project’s external dependencies.
before: Open the project or app folder whose dependencies you want to inspect. A service can exist in the product without being recognizable to the detector.
steps: Open Orbit → Integrations and read the detected service entries.
Use the available entry details as clues to the relevant package or configuration in Code.
Confirm how the application actually uses the service before changing its configuration or asking an agent to modify it.

If the view says No integrations detected, inspect the project scope and its dependency or platform configuration. The empty state describes detection, not a guarantee that the app has no external services.
After dependency or configuration changes, refresh or reopen the relevant project view and inspect the updated result.
For connection failures, check the application’s actual error and service configuration. Use detection to locate the integration, not to diagnose credentials by itself.
outcome: You have a useful starting map of recognizable services and know which findings still need confirmation in the project.
troubleshooting: The demo screenshot intentionally shows the real empty state. Detection does not create an account, authenticate a connection, verify billing, or test a service endpoint. Nested apps may need their own project scope to make the relevant configuration clear.

title: Create a reusable Orbit module
summary: Define a reusable Orbit module with fields, grouping, and an agent job.
before: Choose one repeatable information need, such as an analytics event lexicon. Decide which field uniquely identifies a record and whether grouping is useful.
steps: Open Settings → Orbit → Add new module. Choose Analytics template for a starting example or Blank module for a new structure.
Give the module a clear Name and Description that explain what its records represent.
Review the grouped-table view and Section field. Use a section such as Area when records should appear under meaningful headings.
Define the fields and their types. The first field is the required record identity; use short text, long text, or list according to the information.
Write the Agent job as concrete instructions: what to inspect, what to maintain, and what requires a decision. Check the template’s assumptions before reusing it.
Save module, return to a project, and add it through Orbit → Add.
Create one example record and try a narrowly scoped agent request before using the module for a larger workflow.
outcome: The module definition is available to projects, with a structure and agent job that match its intended use.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the Analytics template before saving. Defining a job does not run an agent. Later definition changes can affect projects using the module, so review field meaning and existing records before restructuring it.

title: Add a module to a project
summary: Enable a saved Orbit module in the project that should use it.
before: Create the module in Settings → Orbit first. Confirm that you are in the intended project before adding it.
steps: Open Orbit from the project rail. Enable Orbit through Manage if needed.
Choose Add in the Orbit sidebar and select the saved module.
Open the new module under Your Orbit. Its records and grouping appear in the main workspace.
Use Add record to create project-specific content, or prepare an agent request with the module’s slash command.
If the module is missing from Add, open Settings → Orbit and check that it exists and is not archived. If it is already listed under Your Orbit, open it there.
outcome: The module is available in the selected project and can be used for its records and agent context.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows Analytics available in Add after saving its definition. An empty module after adding it is normal: a reusable definition does not automatically discover or populate project records. Adding it also does not install an external service.

title: Create records and organize module views
summary: Create clear records and browse them in a grouped Orbit table.
before: Add the module to the project and understand its field definitions. Mark proposed behavior as proposed rather than describing it as implemented.
steps: Open the project’s module and choose Add record.
Fill the required section and identity fields shown by the form. For the Analytics template, Area groups the record and Name identifies the event.
Complete the remaining fields with concrete details. Enter list values one per line and distinguish verified behavior from an idea or future requirement.
Save record and inspect its row under the expected section.
Use Search records to narrow the table. Clear the search if an expected record disappears from view.
Click a record to edit its fields, then save the correction. Reopen it to check longer content that may be truncated in the table.
outcome: The project has a structured record that is easy to find, review, and reference in an agent request.
troubleshooting: The demo record project_opened is explicitly a proposal, not evidence of working instrumentation. Creating or editing a record alone does not change the application. The visible table may require horizontal scrolling for additional columns in a narrow workspace.

title: Start agent work from an Orbit record
summary: Give an agent an Orbit module and identify the record you want it to work with.
before: Add the module to the intended project and review its Agent job in Settings. The module’s instructions can ask for code and record updates, so make the current request’s scope explicit.
steps: Open the record and note its exact name, section, and relevant requirements.
Open New Agent in the same project. Type a slash and the module name, such as /Analytics, then choose the Orbit entry from the picker.
Confirm that the module appears as a chip in the composer. Name the record and section in the request so the agent can find the intended item.
Describe the outcome and limits. For a first review, ask for analysis only and explicitly prohibit code or record changes.
Check provider, model, access, and project before sending. Read progress and respond to decisions that need your input.
Review the result and reopen Orbit to inspect any intended record updates. If implementation was requested, also inspect changed files and test the application behavior.
Send a focused follow-up for missing or inaccurate information. A maintained record and a verified implementation are separate outcomes.
outcome: The agent receives deliberate module context and a clear request about the intended record.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows an unsent Analytics request referencing the proposed project_opened record. Clicking a table row opens its editor; it does not automatically start an agent. Use the module’s slash entry and identify the record in the prompt.

title: Select changes and create a commit
summary: Select the intended files and save a local Git commit.
before: Review the changes and complete the relevant checks first. Confirm whether Git is showing the main project or a Solo workspace.
steps: Open Git → Changes and inspect each file’s diff. Look for unrelated edits, generated files, and private configuration before staging.
Use a file’s checkbox or Stage control to include it. Use Stage All only when every listed change belongs in this commit.
Check the Staged section. Untracked files must be deliberately included; selecting a conversation does not make every repository change part of that task.
Enter a concise commit message describing the result. If you use Generate, review the generated wording before committing.
Choose Commit and wait for the result. Resolve any reported hook, identity, or repository error before retrying.
Open Git → Commits and confirm the new message and commit are present. Return to Changes to inspect anything left uncommitted.
outcome: The selected changes are recorded locally, with unrelated files left out of that commit.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows one staged Markdown file in a demo Solo branch. The example was committed locally and appeared in Commits. A local commit does not push code or create a pull request; those are separate actions.

title: Ship work to a branch and pull request
summary: Review the branch, file scope, and pull-request settings before shipping agent work.
before: Complete the work’s review and tests. Pushing or opening a pull request requires the intended remote repository and an authenticated account with access.
steps: Open Ship from the implementation conversation. Confirm the repository and whether you are working in the main project or a Solo branch.
Choose Current or New branch. Review the branch name and select the intended changes: This chat narrows the candidate scope, while All changes can include unrelated work.
Inspect every selected file and deselect anything outside the task. Resolve any warning about staged changes outside the chosen scope.
Choose whether to Push to remote and Open pull request. When opening a PR, confirm its Base branch and review the proposed title and description.
Leave Auto off when you want a review step. Choose Generate content, then inspect the prepared branch, commit message, and PR content.
Use the final action only when its selected commit, push, and PR effects match your intent. Read the result and follow the PR link when one is created.
If a later stage fails, inspect what already succeeded before retrying. A commit may exist even if a push or PR creation failed.
outcome: The intended changes are delivered to the chosen branch, with a pull request when selected and supported.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the preflight form with three implementation files; it is not evidence that this demo code was pushed. Auto combines preparation and execution, so review its effects before enabling it. Shipping a Solo branch and Rejoining it into a local target are different workflows.

title: Track pull requests and workflow checks
summary: Find pull requests and inspect the progress of Choro Git Workflows.
before: Use the intended repository with a supported remote and account access. Git Workflows require a secure GitHub origin and its connected GitHub CLI account.
steps: Open Git and use the view menu to choose Pull requests. Confirm the repository when your project contains more than one.
Read the PR’s status, number, and source-to-base branch direction. Open its row to inspect the PR on the hosting service.
Review the latest checks, requested changes, and merge requirements on that PR. A successful older run does not establish the status of a newer commit.
Choose Workflows to inspect Choro’s saved branch-promotion workflows and their current or recent runs.
Read the workflow route and completion policy. Confirm before merge waits for a decision; Auto-merge when ready has different effects and still depends on GitHub protections.
For a blocked or failed run, read the reported reason and inspect the associated PR before retrying or reviewing a merge.
If the view cannot load, check repository selection, remote configuration, and account access. An authentication or missing-remote error does not mean there are no pull requests.
outcome: You can connect a local change to its PR and distinguish review, checks, and workflow completion.
troubleshooting: The screenshot identifies the Git views. Choro Git Workflows promote committed work between remote branches through pull requests; they are not the same thing as an individual GitHub Actions job. Starting or merging a workflow changes remote state, so inspect its route and policy first.

title: Understand when to use Solo
summary: Choose Solo when work needs its own branch and working folder.
before: Use a Git project and choose a task with a clear boundary. Consider how the result will eventually be reviewed and brought back.
steps: Use a normal agent for work that should share the current project files with other activity.
Choose Solo for an independent change, experiment, or parallel task whose edits should remain in a separate working folder.
Before starting, check the source branch. Solo begins from its selected Git base; do not assume unrelated uncommitted main-project edits are included.
After the task starts, use the Solo badge and branch strip to identify its scope. Inspect its files through the Solo Git view.
Review and test the result in that scope, then use Rejoin when you want to merge it into a local target branch. Use the separate Ship flow when delivering a branch remotely.
outcome: You have chosen a workspace boundary that keeps parallel file changes understandable.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows one added file in a Solo Git view. A separate working folder is not a security sandbox: agents can still have configured tool or network access. Services, databases, and external accounts can remain shared even when source files are isolated.

title: Start an isolated Solo workspace
summary: Start an agent task in an isolated Solo workspace.
before: Add a Git project and ensure the intended source branch contains the baseline the task needs. Save or commit relevant main-project work through your normal workflow first.
steps: Open New Agent in the intended project and describe a bounded outcome.
Enable Solo beside the branch controls before sending. Review the source branch and any setup options offered by your build.
When setup profiles are available, choose Full setup for prepared environment and dependencies, or Code only when you need just the worktree. Check what your project needs to run.
Check the provider, model, access level, and task limits, then send the request.
Wait for Solo preparation to finish. Confirm the Solo branch strip appears in the conversation before relying on isolation.
Read the result and open Git to inspect the Solo’s own changed files. Keep the task’s review separate from unrelated main-project work.
outcome: The agent works in its own branch and folder, and its conversation retains the Solo scope.
troubleshooting: The demo request adds only a navigation-review document. If setup fails, read the preparation error and check the Git repository, source branch, and required dependencies before retrying. A prepared dependency folder does not guarantee that every service can run without additional configuration.

title: Switch between your main project and Solo work
summary: Move between the main project and Solo work without confusing their file scopes.
before: Keep both conversations available in the project sidebar. A Solo has its own branch and folder even though it belongs to the same project.
steps: Select the Solo conversation and read its Solo branch strip.
Open Git and use the scope strip to select the Solo or main project. Inspect the selected label before staging, committing, or opening a diff.
Select the normal project conversation when you want to continue work in the main folder. Recheck the active scope after switching.
When running or previewing a Solo app, use its own preview controls and confirm the actual service URL and port. An existing main-project server can still be running.
Return to the Solo conversation to continue its task. Switching views by itself does not merge its changes into the main project.
outcome: You can inspect and continue each work stream while knowing which files and branch each action affects.
troubleshooting: The Git screenshot includes separate main and Solo scope choices. Do not use the project’s unchanged top-level branch label alone to infer a Solo’s working branch; read the selected Git scope and Solo strip as well.

title: Review changes in a Solo workspace
summary: Review the changes produced inside a Solo workspace before bringing them back.
before: Let the current agent pass finish and keep the intended requirements available. Review the working tree as well as the agent’s summary.
steps: Select the Solo conversation and read its result, remaining limitations, and any manual checklist.
Open Git → Changes and select the Solo scope. Open each file’s diff and confirm the work matches the requested boundary.
Inspect new and untracked files as well as modifications. Exclude unrelated material from any commit.
Run appropriate checks inside the Solo folder. If you preview an app, confirm the server belongs to that Solo and that it uses the intended configuration.
Ask for focused corrections in the Solo conversation, then repeat the relevant review.
When ready, choose the delivery path deliberately: Rejoin for a local target branch or Ship for the configured remote workflow.
outcome: You have assessed the actual Solo changes and know what will be delivered.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows an untracked Markdown file’s eight added lines in Git. Diff and repository state are stronger evidence of what changed than a short agent summary. A clean working tree after committing still needs comparison with the target branch before Rejoin.

title: Rejoin Solo work with your target branch
summary: Bring reviewed Solo work into a chosen local branch.
before: Finish reviewing the Solo and preserve unrelated work in the target project. Read the Rejoin dialog carefully: successful completion includes removing the Solo working folder.
steps: Open the Solo conversation and choose Rejoin in its branch strip.
Read the confirmation and choose Merge into. If you select a different target, note that the project will switch to that branch.
Confirm that the target is correct and the Solo work is ready. Rejoin creates a merge commit; it keeps the branch and conversation and does not push.
Choose Rejoin when you are ready for the merge and Solo-folder cleanup. Wait for the reported outcome instead of starting a second attempt.
If conflicts pause the operation, use the conflict card to review and resolve them before retrying. The paused-conflict state leaves the target untouched.
After Rejoin complete, inspect the target branch and run the relevant checks there. Continue the conversation on the target project if more work is needed.
outcome: The reviewed work is merged into the selected local branch and the conversation continues in that project scope.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the confirmation before execution. A merged result with cleanup incomplete is different from Rejoin complete; inspect the message and use the offered cleanup action only when appropriate. Rejoin does not publish the branch or create a pull request.

title: Resolve a conflict during Rejoin
summary: Resolve overlapping changes when Rejoin pauses on a conflict.
before: Read the Rejoin outcome before taking another action. Preserve both versions of the work and avoid forcing a merge merely to clear the message.
steps: When Rejoin pauses, read the conflict card’s target branch and list of overlapping files. The card explains that the target was not touched.
Inspect the intended behavior on both sides. Give the agent any product decision needed to combine the changes correctly.
Choose Have the agent sort it to hand the conflict context to the Solo agent, or Not now when you need to investigate first.
Review the resolution in the Solo folder. Check the combined behavior and run the relevant tests; removing conflict markers alone is insufficient.
When the work is ready to rejoin, choose Rejoin again and confirm the intended target in the dialog.
Read the final outcome and inspect the target branch after completion. If the target changes again, a new conflict may need another review.
outcome: The conflict is resolved deliberately in the Solo before the merge is retried.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the Rejoin target-confirmation step, not a simulated conflict result. Distinguish a conflict pause from an authentication, dirty-target, or cleanup error and follow the actual message. Do not discard one side’s changes unless that is the intended resolution.

title: Connect and inspect a project database
summary: Add a project database connection and inspect its tables or collections.
before: Use a database you are authorized to inspect. Prefer a development database and choose Read only when you only need to browse.
steps: Enable DB through Manage if it is absent from the project rail, then open DB → Add DB connection.
Choose Add connection and the provider that matches the database. Fill its provider-specific fields; for SQLite, choose an existing local database file.
Give the connection a recognizable name and choose its access level. Read only exposes browsing and filtering without edit actions.
Use Test connection and read the result. Correct the path, endpoint, authentication, or connectivity issue before saving.
Save the connection, expand it in the Database sidebar, and select a table, view, or collection.
Inspect the records and the access label. For a relational table, use a filter such as status=In review; separate multiple column=value conditions with semicolons.
Use refresh and pagination as needed. If you later enable edits, confirm the database and record before writing; read-only views and tables without suitable keys may remain noneditable.
outcome: The project has a named connection and you can inspect the intended data with an explicit access level.
troubleshooting: The screenshot uses a separate local database containing three fictional projects. SQLite setup requires an existing file; Choro does not create a missing one from the path. A successful connection test does not make every table writable or guarantee that you selected the correct environment.

title: Discuss your project with Project Talk
summary: Talk through your project, ask follow-up questions, and turn a discussion into a plan when you are ready.
before: Select the project you want to discuss. In Settings → Voice, install the local speech models and allow microphone access when macOS asks. A connected coding provider is needed to answer project questions.
steps: Check the active project before starting. Project Talk keeps the discussion tied to that project.
Press ⌘⇧A to start Project Talk. If you changed shortcuts, find Assistant in Settings → Keyboard shortcuts; its description identifies the read-only project conversation.
Wait until Voice is ready and listening, then ask a concrete question, such as “How is navigation organized in this project?” Read the response as well as listening to any spoken feedback.
Continue with a follow-up such as “What would need to change for keyboard navigation?” Project Talk keeps context from the continuing conversation.
To turn the discussion into planned work, say “Create a plan for that” or “Create a plan for” followed by the topic. Inspect the resulting plan conversation before deciding to implement it.
End the session with ⌘⇧A again or say “Stop listening.” Check that listening has ended before moving to an unrelated conversation.
outcome: You can explore the project without starting implementation. An explicit plan handoff creates a separate planning conversation for review.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the actual Voice settings and Project Talk shortcut before speech models are installed. If Voice stays in loading or error, inspect model installation and microphone permission first. Spoken feedback can be Minimal, Balanced, All, or Off; Off does not mean the written response failed. Audio recognition runs locally, while the coding provider processes the text and project context needed for its answer.

title: Dictate and edit a message
summary: Insert spoken text into an agent message, correct it, and send it when it is ready.
before: Prepare Voice in Settings and open the intended agent chat or New Agent composer. Confirm the project and conversation before dictating, because the recognized text goes to that target.
steps: Open Settings → Keyboard shortcuts and search for dictation. Check the bindings for Dictate with voice and Hands-off dictation.
For one message, hold ⌘L while speaking and release it when finished. Wait for transcription to insert the text into the open composer.
Read the transcription. Correct names, file paths, punctuation, and any instruction that speech recognition misunderstood before sending.

Use the normal Send control after checking the draft. Avoid ending your spoken draft with “send” or “send it” if you want to review it first: Choro recognizes a trailing send command and can submit the message.
For continuous input, use ⌘⇧L to start Hands-off dictation and use the same shortcut to stop. Keep an eye on the selected conversation and the listening state.
After stopping, check the final message and the conversation’s response. Dictation changes how you enter text; the agent’s provider, model, access level, and project still govern the request.
outcome: Your spoken text becomes an editable agent message. You can review and correct ordinary dictation before deliberately sending it.
troubleshooting: The screenshot shows the real shortcut controls, not a fabricated transcription. If Choro asks you to open an agent chat, select a valid composer before retrying. If you release the shortcut while the speech model is still installing, wait for installation and dictate again. Stop continuous dictation before switching tasks or discussing unrelated material near the microphone.

title: Run work verification and request fixes
summary: Check finished work against its written requirements, then request focused fixes for clear misses.
before: Work verification is available for eligible agent work linked to a task, doc, or implemented plan with changed files. It is separate from Code Review and from the manual What to check checklist.
